president of the european central bank. - mr president, i have already touched upon many of the problems raised again in this house this afternoon in my opening speech. so, if you will allow me, i will try to group together several of the questions raised by parliament and answer them in a general way, or at least make some comments. let's start with the transparency problem. although i am pleased to learn that the request for the publication of the votes or minutes by the governing council is not included in the motion for a resolution which will be put to the vote tomorrow in this parliament, i must admit that the debate has focused, more than i expected, on the issue of transparency, and even on the publication of the votes. i would like to emphasize one point: when we talk about transparency and call for it, we must clarify what this concept covers. what do we mean by transparency? we must be careful not to confuse transparency with the publication of votes. as regards transparency - which i would define as the provision of the maximum amount of information to the public or parliament on economic and monetary developments and the outcome of the deliberations of the governing council - i think, as i stressed in my introductory speech, that the european central bank can look any central bank in the world straight in the eye. take for example the publication of the considerations which were taken into account in the governing council's final decision on whether or not to change interest rates, which takes place immediately after the governing council meeting. this publication takes place approximately one hour after the decision. this gives us an opportunity to present arguments for or against certain decisions. i don't think you'll find any central bank in the world that is more transparent than we are. the only thing we don't do is publish the votes. apart from the fact - which may be a little embarrassing - that we almost never vote in the governing council and therefore there is nothing to publish, i shall not go back to the arguments against this principle, arguments which i have already made in this house. however, it should be borne in mind that the decisions of the governing council of the escb are taken collectively and that only one decision is made public. the arguments for and against shall be presented at the press conferences and published in the monthly bulletin following the meetings held; but the decision is one. let us not forget that every word spoken by myself or by any member of the governing council on economic developments or on decisions and policies adopted has an immediate impact on billions of euros worldwide. in any case, this word acts as a signal for the market direction and takes effect almost as soon as it is uttered. as for the forecasts, mr president, there is no need to add anything to what i said in my opening speech. we will publish forecasts at some point, on a semi-annual or quarterly basis. i don't know yet exactly what form it will take. we are actively considering this at the moment but we are not ready and we do not have enough data. and we don't yet know what models we will ultimately adopt. we have not yet reached the degree of stability which would allow us to publish reliable forecasts today, but as i said in my introduction, i am sure that this will be done within the next year. i want to avoid any misunderstanding. the following question - which i believe is also the motivation behind the motion for a resolution - has been asked several times in this house: 'why do you not follow the example of the federal reserve system which publishes forecasts?' there must be a misunderstanding here because what the federal reserve releases twice a year in its humphrey-hawkins testimony to the senate is just a range of numbers on a few indicators, a range based on the individual forecasts of the federal reserve's monetary policy committee (fomc) members from the regional federal reserve member banks. it's this range, sort of a forecast presented every six weeks in washington, that gets published. forecasts are also prepared (by the staff of the board of governors) for fomc meetings and in particular for the board of governors of the federal reserve system. these forecasts serve to support the decisions taken by the fomc at a given time. these forecasts are not published. finally, i have already referred in my introduction to the relative influence of forecasts, even if they are published, on the decision-making process. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a welcome step towards the creation of a european patent. at least that's how i understood the question, as a signal that was sent to me. first, the treaty on the functioning of the european union explicitly obliges the ecb to focus on its primary objective of maintaining price stability. the treaty states 'without prejudice to the objective of price stability'; i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. let me make one other small point, mr president, which is important in the context of a motion for a resolution. i think that the terms used in the treaty are being interpreted slightly wrongly. the resolution says "provided that this objective (price stability) is achieved". the treaty, for its part, emphasizes - and not without reason - 'without prejudice to the objective of price stability', and this wording is of paramount importance in economic terms. the terms used in the resolution can be interpreted to suggest that when the inflation rate is below 2%, the escb would be obliged to support the general economic policies of the community. the phrase 'without prejudice' clarifies the situation and that is its purpose: the escb is under no obligation to react in this purely mechanical way if it considers that this could be detrimental to future price stability. i ask the house to take this into consideration. as regards the question of excessive concentration on price stability, i would answer formally that this is part of our mandate. i would also like to reiterate that we do not overestimate the impact that monetary policy can have - what it can and cannot do. i firmly believe that monetary developments can and will influence price fluctuations in the medium term but not in the short term. that is why our strategy is forward-looking. the direct impact of monetary policy on employment and growth is very limited. this is corroborated by studies we have done in the institution where, as mr van den berg has said, i have previously worked. to return to the present situation, i would repeat that the monetary policy strategy, which is being pursued within the framework of the escb and which has been very clearly set out before this parliament, is based on two pillars, both of which have a vision that goes beyond the medium term. these two pillars are: the reference value for monetary growth (m3) and an assessment based on a wide range of indicators and their impact on the primary objective of price stability. this assessment covers a wide range of indicators, including, of course, developments in the real economy, movements in employment and unemployment, an assessment of exchange rate fluctuations if they have an impact on price levels within the euro area. that's our strategy. it's facing the future. of course, we also follow the current trend in inflation because we believe that it gives an indication of what may happen in the future, but it is absolutely wrong to say that we are only relying on the current rate of inflation, as the motion for a resolution suggests. you will understand that i will not enter into the debate in parliament on the short-term decisions to be taken on interest rates, although several members have alluded to this decision. several members of the european parliament have said in this house that if interest rates were to be raised it would hamper economic growth and employment growth. but please remember that when you are driving a car at full speed and you want it to go, but perhaps a little slower, you have a choice between braking or putting your foot on the gas. there's a difference. raising interest rates in a given situation may be more like lifting the foot off the accelerator pedal than slowing down economic momentum and thereby slowing down. we all want to move forward. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the establishment of a european centre for the development of vocational training (ecvet) in the field of vocational training. i hope i've been as clear as i can about the bank notes. previously, the escb explicitly informed the general public that the emergency provision of liquidity to financial institutions in difficulty over a short period of time would not be a problem, provided that the money made available to banks, for example, or other organisations was not put into circulation before 1 january 2000 - the date on which the banknotes would be officially put into circulation. we have stated this as follows: the banknotes may be made available to these institutions provided that legal or contractual guarantees prevent their circulation before 1 january. contracts or legal arrangements will need to be made with retail organisations or banks. so this cash-out would be possible. as regards coins - you know that i have no jurisdiction in this matter, which is the responsibility of the finance ministers - the big difference is that it is almost impossible to obtain the same guarantees for coins, since they are generally put into circulation by the retail sector and not by the banks. it is impossible to obtain these guarantees. another major difference is that it is very easy to counterfeit banknotes with modern photocopying techniques . for this reason, the exact characteristics of future banknotes will be published on a large scale, but only a very short time before their introduction. the aim is to reduce the risk of counterfeiting and to avoid disturbing a public that is not yet familiar with banknotes. coins are much harder to counterfeit. i have addressed all the major issues that have been raised today concerning banking supervision. it is well known that the treaty confers on the european central bank very limited powers in the field of banking supervision. our task is to promote financial stability and financial markets. we monitor this banking supervision, but it is not the responsibility of the central bank. developing new rules is one of our priorities. mr goebbels said the ecb should be "a little less timid on the international stage". the ecb now participates in all discussions in all international forums on what is now called the global 'financial architecture'. the ecb participates fully in all discussions of the g7, the g10 and the oecd. our permanent representative to the imf takes an active part in the discussions within the framework of this organization. the first meeting of the new group of 20 will take place in december, at the instigation of the g7 countries, bringing together the g7 countries and some representatives of the emerging markets. the ecb will also be there. we will also participate in the dialogue. as mr van den berg has asked, we are taking part in the macroeconomic dialogue, just as the central bank in the netherlands is taking part in the dialogue, but without accepting any compromise on its policy in order to obtain concessions in another policy area. no ex ante coordination will be provided; however, all parties concerned, including the ecb, will be engaged in a thorough and, i hope, constructive exchange of information.
commission - (da) mr president, the commission has today approved a communication to parliament and the council on the evaluation of the echo programme. the commission's assessment is based on an expert report, which is therefore written by professionals. i think that's the way it should be. in future, when the commission assesses activities in my sector, it will have to be on the basis of modern, professional and transparent methods. the general conclusions of the experts were positive and the commission shares these positive considerations with regard to echo, but we are aware that some things need to be improved. firstly, there is a need to improve cooperation. we need to improve our collaboration with multinational organisations, un agencies and red cross dependent organisations to help the international community respond more effectively and coordinate better in different crises. echo is such a funder that we have a more general co-responsibility in this respect. in other words, we must set higher standards in our cooperation with the organizations that depend on the united nations. we need to have a broader and more concrete approach to the different humanitarian crises. this will have to be done within the framework of the current regulations. secondly, there is the question of our strategy for managing the echo programme. internal improvements will also have to be made. we will have to focus our efforts more on a comprehensive management of the whole cycle and in particular on ensuring effective feedback. we must, in this connection, evaluate results more than our contribution. there are also some points on which we do not agree with the experts' proposals. we do not want to remove the echo logo, for example. the european taxpayers have a right to know who is being helped and there is no reason to conceal the origin of the help from the beneficiaries. but the logo and our desire to ensure the visibility of aid cannot block collaboration with our partners. thirdly, there are policy considerations. in the long term, the commission intends to develop a coherent strategy for the grey area, i.e. the area between genuine humanitarian aid and development work which is more about the future and the long term. there are active international discussions about the so-called transition period and the commission intends to participate actively in these discussions. on the other hand, the commission's internal resources should be mobilised to enable them to replace humanitarian aid in specific cases and in a timely manner. the aim is to provide echo with the opportunity to define a meaningful exit strategy in the context of the various crises. the decision to combine the two portfolios - development and humanitarian aid - will make this easier to achieve, in particular because of the global nature of echo's field of activity and the competence of the commissioner responsible for development policy. we intend to present a communication on this in june 2000. the commission will also launch a discussion on other important policy areas such as conflict prevention, crisis and disaster preparedness and human rights-based humanitarian aid, i.e. humanitarian aid with a stronger focus on the human rights aspect of victims, including women, including rape victims, child soldiers, internally displaced persons and refugees. it is obvious that coherence with the commission's development policy must be ensured in all these areas. we intend to report on these sectors in july 2001. i'm finally coming to a conclusion. echo will remain neutral in all conflicts. this is important in order to help victims of crises. the presence of echo staff in a number of countries is an important element of any effective humanitarian aid policy. echo is an organisation with its own capacity for action and a staff that is motivated and ready to implement the proposed improvements. in any discussion of making changes, it should be made clear that the loyal and motivated staff working for echo is our main asset. i'm looking forward to the results. i intend to visit east timor shortly. it will be an opportunity to see the practical results of echo's work and i can therefore boast of a good collaboration with all our partners.
commission - mr president, the evaluation has made a number of proposals. one of them concerned echo's closer involvement in the field of development cooperation, i.e. an extended presence of the office after the cessation of hostilities. i do not think that this is the right solution, because we are in danger of quickly exhausting resources by the continuous emergence of new conflicts. we must therefore adopt a balanced approach, based on the resources of our general development cooperation policy, but ensuring that these resources take over immediately after the withdrawal of echo. it seems easy, but it's not. in general, it is necessary to combine these solutions, something that many are unable to do. the big problem is that individual countries, although good donors, do not have sufficient resources to maintain a long-term presence in a large number of conflict zones. the european union has a special capacity and responsibility in this respect. we will have to develop our full efficiency at some point to manage this transition phase. that is a requirement.

president of the council. - (fi) madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i am very pleased to be able to speak to you in the european parliament for the first time as prime minister of finland. i would like to congratulate you on your election and wish you success in the work of the new parliament. in our meeting with the president we noted that we have a new parliament, a new commission, a new beginning and above all a new president, in short the institutional context is now, on the whole, more favourable. i would like to thank you, madam president, for the presentation of parliament's views which you made to the tampere council when it began its work. i am convinced that the decisions taken in tampere meet the expectations of the european parliament. the european council adopted both political guidelines and practical measures to make the european union the area of freedom, security and justice provided for in the treaty of amsterdam. i believe that in many respects the results of the tampere council can be considered a success from the point of view of the expectations of the citizens and the development of the european union. of course, expectations cannot always be fully met, but it is good to see that ngos, such as the european council for refugees and exiles, have welcomed the results of tampere. mr sadako ogata, the un high commissioner for refugees, told me in a telephone conversation after the council that unhcr was satisfied with the outcome of the council. i assured mr ogata that we would continue to cooperate with the unhcr also in the implementation of the decisions. the tampere summit was important for the union in many ways. the european council has been diligent in implementing the amsterdam treaty and has made it a reality. at tampere, justice and home affairs were placed at the highest political level in community cooperation. the summit was a significant step towards closer cooperation between member states; it was decided to remove obstacles to cooperation between police and judicial authorities. the member states of the european union have shown their determination to bring union action closer to citizens by addressing gaps and issues of common concern in community cooperation. at tampere, the union strengthened the foundations for cooperation in the fields of justice and home affairs, which is essentially based on respect for international human rights treaties, respect for fundamental freedoms and respect for the rule of law. the european council has defined the results of its work as 10 milestones, which i shall briefly discuss with you. at tampere, a step was taken towards a common policy on asylum and immigration. the european council underlined the fact that the fields of asylum and migration are separate but closely linked. the first milestone set in tampere is the development of a common european policy on asylum and migration. the most important thing is to act on the causes of emigration in cooperation with the countries of origin. in this regard, the european council welcomes the work carried out by the high level group on asylum and migration in the establishment of action plans to address the causes of immigration. this requires an effective foreign policy, cooperation and human rights, trade policy and conflict prevention. it was decided to extend the mandate of the high level group and to establish further action plans. we have decided to work towards the establishment of a common european asylum system. this decision is, in my view, one of the most important steps taken at the tampere summit. the european council has strongly supported the right to asylum by basing the common european asylum system on the full and comprehensive application of the geneva convention. the principle of non-refoulement, whereby no one may be returned to a place where he or she is likely to be persecuted again, was again expressly reaffirmed. the establishment of a common system will of course take time. the commission is, however, invited to draw up a communication within one year on a common asylum procedure and a uniform status for persons granted asylum throughout the union. implementing the tampere decisions will make it possible to significantly improve the functioning of the asylum system and fairness in europe. the setting of the objective that third-country nationals legally resident in the union should be guaranteed rights and obligations comparable to those of union citizens was an important outcome of the tampere summit. in particular, the legal status of long-term residents in the european union needs to be improved, for example by guaranteeing their right to reside, study, work as an employed or self-employed person. the european union must also defend its most important values in the face of intolerance and exclusion. this is certainly something that is now being given special importance in the european parliament too. the european council stresses the need to strengthen action against racism and xenophobia and invites the member states to draw up national programmes to this end. important decisions were taken on the management of migration flows. it was decided to take measures to combat illegal immigration and the smuggling of persons into the countries of the community. the sanctions against those involved in trafficking in human beings and the economic exploitation of migrants will be made more severe and the action against criminal networks will be strengthened in cooperation between the member states and europol. i would like to stress here that, at the same time, the rights of the victims of these practices will be guaranteed, with particular attention being paid to the problems faced by women and children. cooperation between border control services and between member states will be improved, in particular in the form of exchange and technology transfer programmes. in this respect, the emphasis is on the role of the schengen acquis and the surveillance of external borders in the enlarging union. the european council also agreed on practical measures to build a genuine european area of justice. we decided to create an easy and constantly updated employment information system that would allow citizens to find out about the legal systems of other member states. the union will adopt, on the basis of commission proposals, minimum standards ensuring an appropriate level of legal aid for cross-border cases. at the same time, we decided to simplify and speed up the settlement of disputes concerning small claims in civil and commercial matters and maintenance claims. the rights of victims of crime will be improved through the establishment of minimum standards for the protection of victims, in particular with regard to access to justice for victims and their right to redress. after a thorough discussion, the european council adopted the mutual recognition of judicial decisions and judgments as the cornerstone of the european area of justice. i consider it a positive achievement that the principle of mutual recognition has been adopted in both civil and criminal matters. an important milestone was reached in tampere with the decision to bring civil law and civil proceedings closer together to facilitate judicial cooperation and improve access to the law. the tampere summit was largely concerned with common measures to combat crime at eu level. the european council was unanimous in saying that efforts should be made to better control and hold accountable those persons and organisations who abuse the freedoms within the european union and infringe the rights of citizens, by enhancing cooperation between authorities. the fight against crime must start with improving preventive action. member states will develop national crime prevention programmes and strengthen mutual cooperation and comparison of best practice. the european council calls for the possibility of financing from community resources a programme whose priorities would be youth crime, urban crime and drug-related crime, which have grown the fastest. the decisions taken in tampere have served to build cooperation at european level between police and judicial authorities. the european council decided to set up joint investigation teams to combat drug trafficking, human trafficking and terrorism as a first step. the operational liaison structure at the level of european police service heads will exchange experience and contribute to the organisation of operations in cooperation with europol. europol should also be empowered to request member states to initiate, conduct or coordinate investigations. the fight against organised crime will be strengthened by the creation of a new unit, eurojust. this unit will be composed of prosecutors, magistrates or police officers with equivalent competence seconded by each member state in accordance with its legal system. this will make it easier to ensure that a criminal investigation launched on the basis of europol investigations leads to the indictment and conviction of criminals. a european police college will be set up to train senior police officers and should also be open to officials from the candidate countries. the european council also decided on the approximation of national laws in certain areas of criminal law. the aim is to agree on a common definition of crimes, on the charges and on the penalties. this work should initially focus on a limited number of forms of crossborder crime such as financial crime, drug trafficking, trafficking in human beings, including the exploitation of women, the sexual exploitation of children, high-tech crime and environmental crime. finally, as a final milestone, which i consider to be particularly important in the tampere decisions, we must mention the specific action to combat money laundering. the importance of this action is reinforced by the fact that money laundering plays a central role in organised crime and is closely linked to drug trafficking, human trafficking and the illegal arms trade, amongst others. i would like to stress in particular that judicial authorities and financial intelligence units should be entitled, independently of the confidentiality provisions applicable to banking and other commercial activities, to receive information if it is necessary in the context of money laundering investigations. europol's competence will be extended to money laundering in general, irrespective of the type of offence that is the source of the laundered proceeds. member states shall endeavour to define in a uniform and sufficiently broad manner the scope of criminal activities constituting major offences in the field of money laundering. the objectives set for cooperation in the fields of justice and home affairs can only be achieved by global action. the european council therefore adopted political guidelines on how to strengthen the european union's external action with a view to achieving the objectives in the area of justice and home affairs. the results achieved in cooperation between the baltic states are an example of regional action in the fight against organised crime. the tampere council attached particular importance to closer cooperation in the balkan region. the implementation of the tampere decisions will start immediately, but it will of course take time. monitoring will be carried out in accordance with a methodology which has proved its worth in the implementation of the internal market. the commission will draw up a proposal for a scoreboard to monitor progress in implementing decisions and meeting deadlines. a wide-ranging debate to assess progress will take place at the european council meeting in december 2001 under the belgian presidency. madam president, if i may, i would like to briefly describe the most important objectives which we still want to achieve during the finnish presidency. the most important decision of the helsinki european council concerns the future of all of europe. at tampere, my conviction was strengthened that member states have a very similar conception of how the enlargement of the european union should proceed. the political impetus of the process must not be allowed to wane. the finnish presidency wants to ensure that all candidate countries are encouraged and supported in the same way in their efforts to meet the accession criteria. each candidate country must advance in this process on the basis of its own resources. we want to ensure that the best prepared countries can make faster progress in the negotiations than others. we remind the applicant countries that accession is not possible until the copenhagen criteria for accession are met. i am convinced that on the basis of the recommendations published by the commission on 13 october it will be possible to reach decisions in helsinki based on a comprehensive, credible and coherent policy. this is essential if the positive effects of the enlargement process on europe's stability are to be ensured. but the union must also be renewed. we discussed this with the president this morning. the process of strengthening europe must not have a weakening effect on the decision-making of the european institutions and thus on the union's power to act. i will present to the helsinki european council a report on the necessary institutional reforms to be adopted at the intergovernmental conference in 2000. the finnish presidency will follow the instructions of the european council: prepare a short-agenda igc. however, a wider debate will be needed in the coming years to determine what kind of europe we want, so that we can better respond to the challenges ahead. i do not want to speculate here about when the member states will be ready to move forward more ambitiously and to revise the treaties to further develop the union. the need for deeper reform is growing, both because of enlargement and because of the evolution of the external world. strengthening the common foreign and security policy and developing the european union's crisis management capabilities are among our most important objectives. the european union has the potential to become a strong international player because it has a wide range of political and economic instruments and resources. the common foreign and security policy is currently being consolidated by common strategies. to be a credible actor in maintaining peace and stability, the european union also needs civilian and military crisis management capabilities. the report we will present to the european council in helsinki will examine an approach to conflict management that integrates both civilian and military means. we want to see concrete progress in the development of the common foreign and security policy and decisive steps taken quickly. in conclusion, i would also say that as the country holding the presidency of the european union, we want to improve the efficiency of the european union's action and its transparency. this issue plays a key role if citizens are to be involved in the european union's action. during our presidency we began to reform the council's work. we have improved the transparency of council work, commission. - (el) i should like to begin by addressing a point that has been raised: are we discussing today just one particular company and are we justified in doing so or not? it is clear to me that the michelin case raises two questions which are at the very heart of the problems facing the european union at the moment: competitiveness on the one hand and social cohesion on the other. comparisons with other countries and continents were made to collect examples. and i think we do have lessons to learn from the united states of america in terms of monetary policy, in terms of the use of advanced technology and operational speed at this level, but there is naturally a great difference with europe whose cultural, social and historical model is based on powerful social forces and on a balance between society and the economy. it has been said that europe must create an environment for our businesses. but we must also have a corresponding environment for our citizens, and both will have to be established at the same time. i think that in the course of the very lively debate we have had, this problem is found in both points of view, although, of course, the means are different. can the european union intervene? i think so, because the market is not governed by natural laws, it is not a natural phenomenon. we need political forces to intervene. and we in parliament and the commission are part of these political forces in europe. so i will say that at the level of the european union, there are three levels of intervention. the first level is the area of legislation and institutional interventions. parliament has already put forward proposals on the two directives you have mentioned, one on the european works council and the other on collective redundancies. according to an initial assessment, they have been effective, but the amendments tabled by parliament are currently being reviewed and we will be able to have a debate on these two directives in january 2000. secondly, the directive on information and consultation of workers is already on the agenda of the council of ministers, as you know. i think that at the stage at which we are working to promote it, it would not be appropriate to change it. but this is certainly one of the issues on which the european parliament will have to play an important role. in addition, in this area of institutional and legislative intervention, i think that the proposals to shift the taxation of labour costs and the taxation of workers to the environment are of great interest. there is already a first encouragement to this effect in the employment directives. i believe that at this level, within the general framework of the broad economic guidelines or the employment guidelines, we can draw many lessons from the national level and create a reference base, an exchange of information and successful models which are applied at national level to tackle this enormous problem of restructuring which we face in all areas. we have spoken of the banking sector, which is one of these problems, but naturally europe has a great deal of experience and a very long history of such restructuring, from the textile sector and the shipyards to the industries of today. the functioning of the institutions is the second level. i would like to mention the social dialogue, which many of you have mentioned. let me quote some of the contents of a recent document by unice - the union of confederations of industry and employers in europe - entitled 'unlocking europe's job potential - european social policy for the year 2000: the views of enterprises'. the document states, and i quote, that 'european enterprises see themselves as an integral part of society. this means that they are socially responsible, that they consider profit as the main objective of a company, but not its sole raison d'être, that they give priority to the long term in strategic decisions and investment. european companies are concerned about their responsibilities. one of the main challenges they face is the complexity of the demands of the various actors in society - employees, consumers, funders, public authorities, environmentalists and other interest groups". so when some of the social partners - those who have to face global competition and about whom we all agree that they must be helped and protected because we want european companies to be able to compete on the world stage - are the first to express their concern about society and the maintenance of social balance, we have a very strong argument in favour of supporting and developing social dialogue. of course, you will allow me to make a political observation: these positions are not based on humanitarian considerations and certainly not on socialist ideas. they are based on a very realistic assessment that europe, a region where powerful social forces are at work, will be drawn into social conflicts which will have a direct impact on economic stability, in other words on the environment essential for the development of competition and enterprises, if it lacks social cohesion. i therefore believe that the development of social dialogue is of fundamental importance. i would remind you that yesterday the first round of the macroeconomic dialogue in europe opened, with its technical aspect. the political part of the debate will open on 8 november, and for the first time the social partners who express their concerns about employment, the representatives of the banks who express monetary policy and those of the member states who are the political forces of europe will be gathered around the same table. i believe that it is very important to support and encourage this social dialogue, but that it is also, at the small scale of each company, the prerequisite for any restructuring. and that brings me to the third question: actions and policies. at european level, there is a community strategy for employment, which is being implemented for the first time, with 22 directives that have been incorporated into the employment plans of the member states, and there is also significant funding, which i have already mentioned. these broad lines and the financing of several of these policies include many of the proposals put forward in this forum, such as special tax breaks for workers and smes, support for the training or retraining of workers in the event of redundancy or restructuring, a package of measures to strengthen the social fabric in the event of major restructuring, continuing training and the development of new skills among workers to respond to such restructuring. of course, in times of rapid change, measures taken are never enough, yesterday's measures never meet the demands of tomorrow. i would also like to address the question of state aid and how we link it to corporate profits. i think history has shown that companies cannot operate on the basis of laws that fix the number of their employees or the limits of their profits. but it is clear that the political forces can intervene, in the manner i have mentioned, in the area of reinvestment of profits, by determining the extent to which these profits are reinvested in advanced technologies, in environmental protection or in human resources. such guidelines may be adopted and enforced. i therefore believe that in these times of rapid change we have the latitude to make such changes and adjustments every day. we have an exceptional area of cooperation and exchange of views in this area in the european union. in any case, i can assure you that permanent contact with the committee on employment and social affairs and the committee on industry will help the european commission to take new initiatives all the time, with all the flexibility that is needed in this area.

expire on 1 january 1999 in order to allow the european committee for standardisation to complete certain of its work. in this respect, i would like to say that i agree with mr hatzidakis and another speaker and that i regret that the european committee on standards has not yet reached an agreement which would allow member states to legislate in accordance with what should be the final regulation and not be reduced - if today and in the coming weeks we are not able to amend the current directive - to legislate to change the legislation again shortly afterwards, with all the problems that this would entail. this is the short-term application of article 6 (4) which refers to tanks and containers for the transport of class 2 gas. the expiry of this provision is causing problems and we must therefore see how we are going to remedy this situation. we are simply trying to solve a problem which would not be there today if the committee had done its work in a timely and proper manner. the second objective of this proposal is to amend certain provisions on derogations to provide more precision and to change the procedure for their approval. in view of the positive reception of this item, which has resulted in its approval without amendment by parliament, i can only thank you for your cooperation, your study and your work. i would like to mention a few points that were raised in the debate. firstly, it is obvious that a directive is needed because we are amending an earlier directive. in this sense, the standard required to amend a directive is another directive. in a completely different order of things, i would reply to mr pohjamo that directive 96/35 on safety advisers, which will come into force on 1 january 2000, must contribute to the application of legislation on the transport of dangerous goods, make it more transparent and more in line with everything we want. finally, in continuing with mr konrad's speech, i should like to make a brief comment on rail transport capacity and the fact that the commission and the member states are relying on rail. it is true, as you say, that we are faced with a situation of overcrowding in certain regions, with infrastructure which is already heavily used and which is mainly used for passenger transport, which is currently a priority in the railway policy of all the member states. in recent years, when the railways have been invested in our states, it has been mainly in the transport of people. thanks to these remarkable efforts, which have been successful, we now have high-speed trains that run from brussels to paris in just over an hour. but there is the problem of rail freight. i think that is where we are stuck and we have to work because the forecast of expansion of freight transport in the coming years is - fortunately or not, it depends - very important. this expansion will result from increased development and growth in our countries and, in a way, if it does not happen, it would be a bad sign as regards other behaviours of our economy and, therefore, of our society. in this sense, we must improve infrastructure and above all the interoperability of our trains. as mr konrad so well said, when you arrive at a border in a freight train, it may take you six or seven hours to cross the border. but this problem also appears in air transport. for example, if a person drives across the french-german border, no one asks him to identify himself or to indicate that he is crossing the country. on the other hand, if he goes by air, he has to ask for permission to cross, and sometimes when he is granted permission, he is already in another country, having crossed it in the meantime. mr president, i would like to thank you again and say that i hope that we will soon be able to complete the process of this directive, which will give the standards committee the opportunity to do its work properly.

the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject of the future of the internal market. the second reading of this report contains a number of amendments which the commission can support, for example the amendments concerning 'environmentally friendly vehicles', eevs. these eevs are fuel and technology neutral, allowing member states and local authorities to encourage their use through tax incentives. the concept of eevs will accompany any future limit value obligations. therefore, the commission can accept, in principle, to consider extending the scope of the concept of eev to include other automotive characteristics such as noise pollution, fuel consumption and other propulsion technologies. the commission can also support the amendments relating to the extension of the directive to other alternative fuels, ethanol in this case, the amendment on tax benefits for retrofitting old vehicles, the amendment to include commercial vehicles in the overall community strategy on co2 emissions and the amendment on the quality of liquefied petroleum gas. the commission can also support in principle the amendment on the control strategies for abnormal emissions, but we would prefer to postpone the reporting date. a deadline of the end of 2002 would allow the commission to fully assess the effects of the new test cycles which will be introduced next year in the new european vehicle emissions regulation. the council adopted a common position setting stricter limits for particulate matter, thus significantly moving closer to the view expressed by the european parliament at first reading. the commission supports this preventive approach to ultrafine particles. the main problem with this package of amendments is the advance of the date of application of the strict limits for nitrogen oxides, nox. the commission considers that the stage of development of the technology required to achieve such strict nox limits makes it difficult to accept a date earlier than october 2008. in this respect, a feasibility study is necessary, as emission control arrangements to achieve the ambitious nox limits are still being developed. although laboratory tests are promising, we have no certainty as to the long-term operational efficiency of these devices, which is necessary if we are to make them a viable and sustainable technical solution to ensure emission control. there are also important problems to be solved in the field of fuel quality, in particular sulphur content. in conclusion, the commission can accept the following amendments: the first part of amendment no 3, amendments nos 6, 7 and 10, amendments nos 16 to 26 and amendments nos 29 to 47. the commission can accept in principle amendments nos 1, 4, 5, 13, both parts of amendment no 12 and amendment no 15. the amendments which the commission cannot accept are amendment no 2, the second part of amendment no 3, amendments nos 8 and 9, the two parts of amendment no 11 and amendments nos 14, 27 and 28.

- the following reports by mr lechner, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties and internal affairs, on the proposal for a council directive on the service in the member states of judicial and extrajudicial documents in civil or commercial matters (com (99) 219 - c5-0044/1999 - 1999/0102 (cns)) are requested for joint debate: - a5-0057/1999 by mr gebhardt, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the proposal for a council regulation on jurisdiction and the recognition and enforcement of judgments in matrimonial matters and the matters of parental responsibility for joint children (com (99) 220 - c5-0045/1999 - 1999/0110 (cns)).
the commission has already adopted a number of proposals for directives on the interpretation and notification of judicial and extrajudicial documents in civil and commercial matters and on the proposal for a regulation on jurisdiction and the recognition and enforcement of judgments in matrimonial matters. i would like to pay special tribute to mr lechner and mrs gebhardt for the excellent work they have done as rapporteurs on these two initiatives. these two instruments are one of the cornerstones of the community edifice we are building, the central objective of which is to give all citizens and legal operators in the union easier, faster and more effective access to justice, while preserving the rules of legal certainty. as regards the proposal for a directive, by reducing the time limits for the service of judicial and extrajudicial documents from one member state to another, we are going to adopt an instrument which will allow judicial proceedings to proceed with the greatest possible speed and legal certainty, while safeguarding the rights of all parties concerned in such cases. i would particularly like to stress the importance of the adoption of the proposal for a regulation, which was a cornerstone of the creation of a european judicial area at community level. in this connection, the tampere european council made the mutual recognition of judicial decisions one of the main lines of development of the area of freedom, security and justice. the heads of state and government themselves have recognised the importance of giving priority to family relations and, in particular, to the settlement of divorce and parental authority. the movement of persons within the european union must be accompanied by the necessary measures in the field of family law. this proposal is the first of these measures, and only the first, because it provides uniform rules on the jurisdiction of the courts of the member states in matters of divorce and legal separation and in matters relating to proceedings for the settlement of parental responsibility. it also provides a clear and consistent framework for the rapid and virtually automatic recognition in each member state of decisions given in another member state falling within the scope of the regulation. these are legal instruments which pave the way for the adoption in the future of other, more profound solutions in the direction desired by the tampere european council. as far as the directive is concerned, the commission accepts virtually all the amendments, with the exception of amendments nos 3, 5 and 10 which do not seem to us to be in line with the logic of the proposal. unless otherwise stated, amendment no 3 does not introduce anything new into the provision in question, since the member states which will designate a single authority, or even a central authority, are precisely those which do not allow direct transmission of decisions in their law. as for amendment no 5, it seems to us that it places an unduly heavy burden on the central authorities in a directive system where these central authorities have only a subsidiary function. finally, as regards amendment no 10, we believe that it is contrary to article 11 (2) of the proposed directive. as for the proposal for a regulation, most of the proposed amendments are acceptable: i am referring to amendments nos 1 to 8, 13 to 18 and 20. we think that amendments nos 9 and 10 are acceptable in part, subject to a slight modification which does not alter their nature. we object to three amendments: amendments nos 11, 12 and 19. as for amendment no 11 - and i am waiting for a new oral proposal to be made so that i can comment on the new version - when it requires that the interests of the child be taken into account, it seems to us that it leaves the door open to a judgment - as to the substance of the part of the state which is supposed to receive the judicial decision - which does not fall within the scope of this type of instrument. we therefore agree on the principle of the hearing of the child, but not on the question of a new judgment on the merits. as for amendment no 12, it seems to us that it favours the automatic execution of a judgment which may be older than a more recent judgment which may have been given on the same question. priority should be given to the most recent judgment, as it will take the child's situation into account when the sentence is carried out. finally, as regards amendment no 19, i understand the meaning of the proposal, but i would draw attention to the fact that the rule on the transposition of judgments does not enter into a regulation on jurisdiction, recognition and enforcement of judgments: the appropriate place for the rule on transposition is in the directive on the transmission of documents, the other instrument we are debating today, which precisely provides for its possibility of transposition. finally, mr president, i am convinced that the adoption of these instruments is giving a great boost to the free movement of persons today. it is given a balanced impulse because it is a question, on the one hand, of promoting the internal market, of promoting economic integration by means of the directive on judicial and extrajudicial documents in civil and commercial matters, but it is also a question, on the other hand, of giving priority to the rights of persons, to the rights of human beings, to the rights of children, who are already suffering from the trauma of divorce, but who should not suffer from the trauma of the bureaucratic drama of the recognition of judicial decisions. finally, it is proof that the union is adding value to the practical lives of our citizens. we are therefore honouring a major value of the european construction project by thinking of people, by people and for people.
- thank you very much, commissioner. the joint discussion is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon.
the agenda calls for the commission to make a statement on the implementation by the commission of the programme for the control of nuclear installations in the countries of central and eastern europe. mr verheugen, on behalf of the commission.
the commission has also adopted a proposal for a very important directive on tobacco. this marks the end of a very long consultation process involving the council and parliament. the main aims of the directive are: to limit the current tar content in cigarettes; introduction, for the first time, of a limitation on the nicotine content, as well as on carbon monoxide; improved quality and larger labels informing about the dangers of smoking and the tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide content of cigarettes; control of misleading use of terms such as 'light' or 'low tar content' etc.; the commission has also proposed new guarantees for tobacco additives. the reasons for the establishment of such a directive are clear. the community has very important public health obligations to fulfil, particularly since the ratification of the treaty of amsterdam. these include the obligation to ensure a high level of health protection in all community policies and activities. smoking kills half a million citizens in the european union each year and is the single most important preventable cause of death. so we need to take strong action to tackle the problem. the directive, when adopted, will provide european smokers with the highest level of protection in developed countries. they will benefit from better information on the composition of their cigarettes and the dangers of smoking. they will also be protected by measures to limit tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide. however, the directive is also proportionate. we have been careful not to stigmatize smokers. we must avoid being too normative and interfering in the daily lives of citizens. the aim is to establish a framework that provides comprehensive information on tobacco and its dangers. this will complement the community's ban on tobacco advertising, which is designed to combat the industry's efforts to attract new smokers, especially young people. the combination of these measures should make smoking a much less controversial issue in the future. i hope that in the future parliament will support the commission's proposal in the co-decision procedure.

question no 45 by mrs ria g.h.c. oomen-ruijten (h-0619/99):is the commission (in particular the commissioners responsible for the environment and agriculture) aware that the european directive on nitrates (91/676/eec) oj l 375, 31.12.1991, p. 1. does not offer a watertight guarantee as regards the quality of groundwater, as it focuses exclusively on nitrates from animal manure and therefore ignores a number of other sources of nitrates? does the commission share the view that, at the moment, it seems almost impossible to implement the directive fully and on time, given that it is causing problems in nine member states? does the commission realise that the monitoring of the application of the directive is not perfect, given that different measurement methods are used within the union? is the commission prepared, given that the implementation of the nitrates directive seems to be causing problems in so many member states, to rethink the improvements and the timing of finally reaching the nitrates standard?
commission. - you ask whether the nitrates directive ignores other sources of nitrates and whether it can be applied. it also concerns monitoring and you ask whether the commission is prepared to reconsider possible improvements. here's my answer. the nitrates directive takes account not only of nitrogen from animal manure but also of chemical fertilisers, both in terms of the quantities provided - i refer to article 5 and annex iii - and the methods and periods of application, contained in annexes ii and iii. the commission is aware of the difficulties faced by several member states in applying this directive but considers it to be an important element of its policy to tackle the problem of water pollution. in this context, the commission will continue to insist on the full application of the directive as requested by parliament in its resolution of 20 october 1998. the commission is preparing monitoring and reporting guidelines with the member states which will allow comparisons, as well as the collection of results and maps from the year 2000 onwards, when the member states will report on their first action programmes. a comprehensive study on eutrophication and the problems of groundwater and the designation of vulnerable areas by the member states has already been carried out by the commission. the tools for a sound management of nitrogen in fields and water runoffs are all available in the existing directive once it is properly applied in all intensive farming and livestock areas in europe.
the commission is of course going to insist that the directive be applied. you might of course wonder whether the commission will not consider a short-term review of the directive. the commission considers that most of the measures to be taken by the member states, such as monitoring transposition, designation and establishment of codes of good practice, action programmes and reports, are the most obvious. most of the measures in annexes ii and iii are proving very effective in reducing losses, for example, of phosphorus from agriculture and the future water framework directive will complement them by making it possible to draw up management plans for runoff. there is therefore no need to draw up new interim directives or to revise existing ones; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject. i think the directive could not be clearer. the problem still exists and is getting worse. so we must continue along this path. we have increased legal pressure - 11 countries are currently involved in high-level infringement proceedings - and the court of justice recently sentenced italy and spain. the situation is changing for the better as a result of the pressure exerted. all countries must now transpose the directive. the vulnerable areas have recently been re-designated for spain, greece, italy and the united kingdom and the content of the action programmes has been strengthened in a number of countries. the situation can therefore be expected to improve in the coming years.

- question no 48 by mr john walls cushnahan (h-0631/99) subject: convention of 1983 on compensation for victims of violent crime the commission has recently invited all member states to ratify the 1983 convention on the compensation of victims of violent crimes. which member states have already done so and what steps does the commission intend to take to ensure that all member states ratify this convention?
commission - (pt) mr president, the commission has recently presented to the council, the european parliament and the economic and social committee a communication on the subject of victims of crime in the european union - reflection on the rules and measures to be adopted. in this text, the commission sets out the elements of a debate on the rules of application for victims of crime in the european union. one of the main elements of the commission's communication is precisely the ratification by all the member states of the 1983 council of europe convention. i can tell you, mr president, that this convention has been ratified by germany, denmark, finland, france, luxembourg, the netherlands, the united kingdom and sweden. some member states have already signed the convention but have not yet completed the process of ratifying the agreement through their national laws. this is the case in belgium, greece and portugal. finally, four member states have not yet signed the convention: austria, spain, ireland and italy. before presenting any proposal for specific action in this regard, the commission invited the member states, at council level and on the basis of the communication in question, and the european parliament, to provide it with their comments on the points addressed in the communication on the protection of victims of crime. i can tell you that the response of the council of ministers for justice and home affairs on 4 october was very positive in relation to this communication. the commission is awaiting the opinions of parliament and the member states in order to draw up the proposals for further action to implement the objectives of the communication to which i have just referred.
commission - i agree with the honourable member. if you look at the tampere european council conclusion 32, it is clear that we have a mandate to suggest concrete measures within the legal framework of the amsterdam treaty. i hope that by the end of the year the member states and parliament will have reacted so that we can immediately propose specific european legislation on this subject at the beginning of the year 2000 and continue to press for the ratification of the 1993 convention.
commission - this is precisely the aim of the evaluation we intend to carry out with the council by the end of this year. at the end of the year we will be able to assess not only the progress made by national legislation to protect victims of violent crime but also the concrete measures that each member state is prepared to implement. these include compensation, psychological and medical treatment, assistance to victims in the recovery of claims, the transmission of decisions from one member state to another with a view to improving the protection of victims or the request to the courts to accept written evidence from victims who cannot attend the trial against their offenders because they reside in another member state. i hope that all these aspects will be examined by the end of the year and will form the basis of the initiative which the commission intends to take in the year 2000.

commission. - (de) mr president, the commission is fully aware of the importance of reforming the social security systems of the applicant countries in the context of their accession to the eu. with the exception of the rights of seasonal workers and the coordination of regulations concerning them, the community acquis is not very extensive in terms of social security. as the commission communication of 14 july 1999 on the modernisation of social security systems shows, the aim is to develop the acquis. the candidate countries will have to be involved in this process. in its annual reports to the council and parliament on 13 october, the commission takes stock of the situation in the applicant countries. the commission notes that modernization is generally very slow in the social and health sectors, but that efforts are being made to establish sustainable social security networks. for example, changes have recently been made to the social security and health care systems of romania, slovakia, slovenia, the czech republic, lithuania, hungary, malta, bulgaria and poland. this is already a considerable effort, but it is not enough. this encourages the commission to continue the implementation of the programmes for the reform of social security systems in the candidate countries. these programmes are called consensus 1 and consensus 2. they should be continued, in addition to the technical assistance which most of these countries have already received through national phare resources allocations. from the year 2000, the reform and modernisation of social security systems in the candidate countries could also be supported by the consensus 3 programme. since 1999, this area has received support of up to eur 18.6 million. these resources are used for institutional improvements in the social sector in the candidate countries, and the partnership policy plays an important role in this. in the context of the accession partnerships, the strengthening of administrative structures, which is essential for coordination in social security matters, is a medium-term priority in romania, the czech republic, hungary, poland, cyprus, slovakia, malta, bulgaria, latvia, lithuania and slovenia. in addition, the european commission has repeatedly pointed out to the candidate countries the useful role that the social partners can play in the accession process and also recalled that a better consideration of social problems made it necessary to develop the social dialogue in these countries.
commission - (de) mr president, the word 'demand' may not be appropriate in this context. we deal with sovereign states. the way we deal with our partners is not one that i would be prepared to call 'demanding', especially when it comes to an area where there is no acquis. we can of course demand, because this forms the basis of the negotiations, that the applicant countries take over everything that is subject to legal regulation in the european union. but what is the fruit of, say, social interaction is not the subject of any legal regulation. in this respect, the political dialogue, which is also a component of the accession strategy, is constantly stressing the need for intensive social dialogue. we have done so in the past, we will do so in the future and i would point out that the practices in this respect are very different and that in no way are the majority of the applicant countries behind the member states' standards in this matter.
- question no 57 by mr jonas sjöstedt (h-0627/99) subject: enlargement of the eu and the schengen agreements accession to the eu will require the candidate countries to integrate the eu acquis on visas and border controls, which will require considerable changes for many of them, including the introduction of visas and increased border controls with neighbouring countries. has the commission carried out a study of the changes which will have to be brought about in the candidate countries with which negotiations have been opened? has a list been drawn up of the neighbouring countries for which the applicant countries will have to introduce a visa requirement? are any derogations or transitional provisions envisaged to facilitate the implementation of these changes?
commission - (de) mr president, on 31 march 1998, following the opening of the accession negotiations, the commission carried out an analytical review of the eu acquis with the candidate countries concerned. chapter 24 of the accession negotiations, which concerns cooperation in the fields of justice and home affairs, dealt with the issue of external border controls and the eu's visa policy. it became clear during the review that further progress was needed to return to the acquis. further reform needs were also identified following expert missions organised by the commission and attended by representatives of the administrative and judicial authorities of the member states. the applicant states are obliged to take up and apply the acquis communautaire existing at the time of accession. this also applies to the list of visas in force at the time of accession, which was drawn up by the council after consulting the european parliament. as regards the question of transitional arrangements which the applicant countries may request in the context of this chapter of the accession negotiations, the basic position of the european union is that such measures are possible only exceptionally and for a limited duration and scope. transitional regulations may not entail any change in the union's regulations and policies, or impair the smooth application thereof, and may not cause any significant distortion of competition.
commission - (de) but of course, mr president, that is the point of the whole matter, subject to certain conditions, however. first condition: we do not want to allow any exceptions to the visa requirement. the council regulation is clear in this respect. if we tolerate exceptions, we would be abandoning the fundamental principle of a uniform area of freedom, security and justice. i should also like to point out, as you have very rightly said, that this is a very sensitive subject. i am very sensitive not only because the implementation will be difficult for the applicant countries but also because i know a number of member states which will not accept enlargement unless there is the greatest clarity on this issue. we need not only the consent of the candidates but also that of the members. and for most members, this is a central point on which they cannot contemplate any compromise. as regards external border controls, the applicant countries are expected to adopt and apply, as i have already said, the acquis communautaire as soon as they join. however, internal border controls will only be abolished once the union has confirmed that the candidate country can fully guarantee the effective implementation of the eu acquis in this area. but your question was whether internal controls would be abolished. the answer is a resounding "yes". that's what this is about.
