commission. - mr president, i should like to begin by congratulating the european parliament on its sense of urgency. this debate on the schwaiger report could not have come at a better time, since we are in the midst of extremely lively discussions on the preparation of the seattle agenda. i would also like to congratulate the union as negotiator on the schwaiger report. its adoption will send a clear signal to our partners that the european union will not be content with a minimalist approach, aimed only at improving market access in a few sectors. this would not meet the concerns of our fellow citizens or the legitimate demands of developing countries. if i believe your speeches today, your vote tomorrow will strengthen our hand, and therefore the union's hand, in seattle. we are all aware that the trade debate has changed the approach we are proposing, and the schwaiger report reflects this. we certainly want to continue the liberalization of trade, which has been and remains a strategic factor in our prosperity. but the next round of negotiations must also address new issues: development, the environment, health and safety, basic social standards, competition and its transparency, minimum investment rules and the promotion of cultural diversity. the sum of all these factors leads us to recommend a wider round of negotiations - and i welcome the very strong agreement between the commission and parliament on this point, as is clear from your report, mr schwaiger. some of you do not share this approach and propose a kind of moratorium on the negotiations. i don't think that's the answer. firstly, because we have commitments to respect in the follow-up to the uruguay round. secondly, we must take account of the risk of a moratorium. if we do not make further progress on the path of multilateral liberalisation, then the door is open to the unilateralism of the strongest. is that really the aim of those who are calling for a moratorium? thirdly, why delay the negotiation of the rules, which our civil society rightly demands and which developing countries expect to incorporate trade liberalisation and sustainable development, in dimensions such as health, the environment and the fundamental rights of workers? i am therefore convinced that this negotiation is necessary, but i also welcome the fact that the conditions for this negotiation have changed compared to the previous round. given the concerns that a growing number of our citizens are expressing about globalisation, we need a wider, more transparent, more interactive public debate. in this respect, i believe that the discussions which accompanied the preparation of the schwaiger report, both within parliament and between parliament and the commission, were exemplary. i therefore pay tribute to mr schwaiger, who has done a herculean job in drawing up a compromise version of your many proposals, which i hope will be voted on tomorrow. i would like to respond to the debate by briefly mentioning some of the issues that were highlighted in the preparation of the report. first of all, with regard to developing countries, it is clear that those countries which have benefited least from the establishment of the wto and the results of the uruguay round are also, without exception, those which have been least integrated into the world trading system. the aim is therefore to encourage their participation with a view to their integration, not to delay it. where the lack of integration is primarily due to a lack of resources or insufficient capacity, then technical and financial assistance should be provided to developing countries to increase their capacity to negotiate and implement wto measures. on the other hand, when the lack of integration is the result of weak internal or development policies, the extension of application deadlines and the multiplication of preferential measures are not the right solutions. while special and differential treatment remains essential for developing countries, it should encourage them to implement sustainable development strategies, not exempt them from them. as regards relations with the acp countries, for example, a new approach is needed, one which must in particular converge towards the rules of the wto, because the current system must in any case be reviewed, even if we have to make the necessary transitions. as regards intellectual property, we are convinced that the rules on intellectual property must enable developing countries to benefit themselves from the resources at their disposal and that the current provisions are already making great strides in this direction. a thoroughgoing revision of the agreement would therefore not be a good thing. on the other hand, if we take an integrated view of the link between intellectual property and development, we must, alongside the extension of its safeguards, ensure that direct investment is encouraged as the main vehicle for technology transfer to these countries, and that agreements on technological cooperation are developed with them and perhaps - i am suggesting this - that we consider strengthening european investment in basic research on living things in order to share the benefits with them. in the field of environment, many concerns focus on the applicability of environmental measures to wto rules. the ideal solution would, of course, be multilateral negotiation of a hierarchy of standards. we know that it is not within our reach. in the meantime, we must work to ensure that each new standard is in line with the previous ones, so that, where necessary, the margin left to the judges who are faced with these discrepancies is not empty. one of our goals is to ensure mutual compatibility in this context, which would allow environmental or other measures to be implemented in accordance with wto rules. the precautionary principle is another matter which is of great concern to some of you. it is clearly up to each wto member to decide whether there is a risk or not. the precautionary principle must then enable it to take proportionate measures to avoid that risk. the important thing for us is therefore to clarify the rules and procedures governing the application of the precautionary principle. i note the concerns that have been expressed about services. i would like to reassure you on this point. in no case am i mandated to accept, as part of an international negotiation, the challenge to the power of union governments to regulate or to be active in these areas. we recognise the essential and crucial role these services play in our society. as far as agriculture is concerned, we are up to now faced with a position of the cairns group which aims to equate agricultural products with other commodities. that is not our position. this was not what was agreed by all the contracting parties in 1994 and what we respected. it will be necessary to start from the concept that agriculture has other functions than producing for the market. let's get down to social norms. globalisation is having its effects on the social sphere in all countries, but it is also clear that in a number of less developed countries the international labour standards agreed under the international labour organisation are not sufficiently respected. the mention of social standards is provoking reactions from some of our partners at the wto, particularly from developing countries, which i can attest are extremely strong. it is therefore essential to begin by reaffirming our opposition to the application of trade sanctions in the social field and to any protectionist use of them. in our view, respect for the fundamental rights of workers is the reason for a more equitable distribution of the gains from growth brought about by trade liberalisation. it is with this in mind that our generalised preferences scheme allows us to grant autonomous reductions to countries which actually apply the main ilo conventions. the important thing for us in seattle - and i think we all agree on this - is to make it possible to discuss the subject in the context of ilo/wto cooperation. i would also like to confirm our support for mr somavia's presence in seattle as a positive signal of the attention that will be given to this matter. a word, mr president, before we conclude, on china. i did not speak publicly on this matter until this debate. is the signing by the americans and the chinese of an agreement on wto accession, as many of you have asked, good news or bad news? first of all, from the point of view of those who question the wto, this is not good news. china, a country whose development is crucial for the future of the planet, is sending a clear signal that it wants to join a multilateral trading system. from the point of view of our multilateral interests and our own interests, everything depends on the content of the agreement that has been signed, since the us congress wanted to have the first look at the content of this agreement, a procedure for which your assembly should have more sympathy than antipathy, even if it complicates my life. i regret that my own information on the details is only available to me in drops. but the devil, perhaps the dragon in this case, is in the details. i have no reason to doubt the good faith of the american negotiators, with whom our negotiators have worked very hard over the last two years on the common interests we share. nor do i have any reason to suspect that concessions on multilateral terms which are important to us were paid for in bilateral currency which has no value for us. if this is not the case, it will be necessary to negotiate with the chinese side on the subjects in which the union has particular interests. in summary, probably good news, but with the benefit of the retail inventory, which is under way. i would like to conclude, mr president, by welcoming the members of your institution who are part of our delegation to the ministerial conference in seattle. this is part of a tradition which i am happy to keep alive. i shall meet tomorrow with your delegates in seattle - and i hope you will have done so by tomorrow - and we can discuss in more detail the arrangements we will be making there.

institutional reform is not a political project. it's a tool. our project, as many of you have said, and which underlies our reflection today, is the bringing together of the peoples of the european states in a political, economic, social and cultural community. the welcome of many new members is therefore the great political project for the very beginning of the next century. that is why the distinction made in amsterdam between a limited adjustment, a small enlargement, and a wider reform is now an outdated distinction. the commission's contribution to the preparation of this conference conference must focus on institutional matters, on all institutional matters, with the notable and politically essential exception of the discussions currently under way on a european security and defence policy. in order to succeed, institutional reforms must, it seems to me - and i say this with the experience i have of the previous negotiations - be placed in a broader political perspective and try to answer together this fundamental question: 'how should we talk to each other? how should we work? and that is the only question we have to ask when we seek the answers, all the answers, listening to the president-in-office of the council speak of enlargement, which he said means 'change'. and i echo him in saying that this is a big expansion, not a small adjustment. and this great enlargement must be met by real reform, which must therefore first of all affect decision-making. that is why i think we will agree, by a majority, that qualified majority voting in the council should become the rule, with exceptions limited to a few fundamental and very sensitive issues. we have also written, as many of you have wished, that when it comes to legislative matters, qualified majority voting should be associated with a co-decision procedure between the council and the european parliament. the second issue is the evolution of the treaties. i raised this idea during my hearing before your parliament. it was taken up and emphasized in the report by jean-luc dehaene, president von weizsäcker and lord simon, and it deserves to be studied in depth. it consists in reorganizing the treaties by separating the basic texts from the implementing texts. this reorganisation would allow the treaties to continue to evolve, since the implementing texts could possibly one day be amended like to say, however, that this reorganization should not, in my view, lead to a change in the current powers of the union or the community. another point is the representation of the states in the council. the council's decisions should be more representative of the relative weight of the different member states of the union. the decision-making process should also be facilitated, while intergovernmental conference. the functioning of the institutions does not necessarily imply a revision of the treaties. in the daily work of the european parliament, the commission and above all the council, there are important reforms of internal structures which will have to be carried out before enlargement. the second major challenge, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, is to prevent the risk of dilution, of dispersion, which we are running together with enlargement. when there is a risk, i repeat before you, either we suffer it, or we accept it as fate, or we prevent it. we want to prevent this risk of dispersion. the treaty of amsterdam has established the legitimacy of certain forms of cooperation between member states within the institutional framework of the union, to go few key areas, including trafficking in human beings. the decision taken in tampere on the extension of europol's powers and on the strengthening of measures against money laundering will also question no 3 by mr marco cappato (h-0557/99): the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. subject: opportunity to finance the united nations programme for international drug control (unidoc) the annual survey on opium production, published by unodcid, shows that the estimated amount of opium produced in afghanistan more than doubled in one year, from 2 100 tonnes in 1998 to 4 600 tonnes in 1999. the area devoted to opium cultivation increased by 43% from 64 000 to 91 000 hectares. in 1999, 97% of the areas where opium is grown were controlled by the taliban and the number of afghan districts where opium is grown increased from 73 to 104. total estimated production rose from 3750 to 6000 tonnes, an increase of 60%. for several years, unctad has been engaged in costly and intensive programmes to eradicate opium crops in afghanistan. these crops are directly managed by the taliban, known for the violent and segregationist regime they have imposed on the country. the eu funds unodc and its programmes, including the one on afghanistan, from its budget. does the council not consider that the eu should suspend its support, including financial support, to the 'taliban project' and conduct a thorough investigation into the effectiveness and sound management of unodc funds? does the council not consider that the use of eu funds by unodc in programmes implemented under schemes that violate the most basic human rights constitutes a serious breach of the principle of conditionality underlying eu action?
counsel. - (fi) mr president, i am pleased to be able to answer the new question put by the honourable member on the financing of the undp. the undp is not funded by the eu budget. the european union supports at a general level the well-established and effective action of the unodc in the field of narcotic drugs and is also very satisfied with its cooperation with the unodc in other areas. as the honourable member has said, action in afghanistan is made difficult by the absence of a government with a large majority and, therefore, of a reliable interlocutor. the european union is working with countries close to afghanistan, in particular those in central asia and iran, to strengthen cooperation in the fight against drugs. the union considers the central asian region to be of strategic importance in the fight against drugs and is currently developing an action plan for central asia. one of the reasons for the current crisis in the drugs sector is the lack of effective border controls between afghanistan, kazakhstan, turkmenistan, kyrgyzstan, uzbekistan, tajikistan and russia. the european union is working to find a solution to this situation by encouraging tacis projects in the context of customs cooperation and justice and home affairs cooperation. the aim of these projects is to improve the effectiveness of border controls between iran, afghanistan, turkmenistan and uzbekistan, as well as to improve the training of customs authorities and to strengthen drug expertise in kazakhstan, turkmenistan, kyrgyzstan, uzbekistan, tajikistan and russia. as regards iran, the european union was informed that the unodc had just adopted a drug control programme for iran under its auspices and had opened an office in the country. the member states are currently studying the arrangements for participating in the financing of this programme.

- question no 7 by astrid thors (h-0559/99): the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the united kingdom for the construction of the new nuclear power station at chernobyl. subject: regulation introducing transparency in the spring of 1999, coreper invited the commission to submit a proposal to implement the provisions of the treaty of amsterdam on transparency. has the council made a similar request to the new commission? would a proposal for a regulation not be preferable to the form proposed last spring, namely a simple communication? what working party in the council will be examining the proposal, an ad hoc group composed of representatives of the ministries of justice, for example, or the information group currently responsible for dealing with requests for documents?
counsel. - (sv) as the honourable member knows, article 255, previously article 191a, of the treaty establishing the european community states: '1. any citizen of the union and any natural or legal person residing or having its registered office in a member state shall have a right of access to european parliament, council and commission documents, subject to the principles and conditions to be laid down in accordance with paragraphs 2 and 3. 2. the the general principles and limits governing the exercise of this right of access to documents, on grounds of public or private interest, shall be laid down by the council, acting in accordance with the procedure referred to in article 251, within two years of the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam. 3. the each institution referred to above shall draw up in its rules of procedure specific provisions concerning access to its documents. " so far, the commission has not presented a formal proposal for a legal act, and consequently the council has not been able to start dealing with the case either. since the general principles and rights governing access to the documents of these institutions must be established by a process of co-decision with the european parliament by 30 april 2001, the council will begin to deal with the proposal for a legal act as soon as it is submitted to it. the working party responsible for examining the commission proposal has not yet been appointed. the chairman of the information group put forward, in his programme on transparency, the idea of an ad hoc group, composed mainly of experts in the field of document accessibility.

mr president, i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. despite considerable efforts to prevent drug use and addiction, the drug problem continues to pose a series of threats and challenges as the year 2000 dawns. the most acute problems are caused by the use of opiates, in particular heroin, amphetamines and the use of several drugs at the same time. cannabis remains the most widely used illicit drug in the union. infectious diseases such as aids or hepatitis b and c have reached high levels of spread among injecting drug users. organized crime is playing an increasingly prominent role in the production and trafficking of drugs. we must rise to these challenges. i must also express my sincere gratitude to the committee on civil liberties and human rights, justice and home affairs and its rapporteur, mrs giannakou-koutsikou, for the quality of their work and the speed with which they recommended the commission's communication on the fight against drugs for the period 2000 to 2004. this will enable the european council in helsinki to adopt an effective strategy against this worrying phenomenon. the main objectives of the european drug strategy over the next five years can be summarised as follows: to significantly reduce the use of illicit drugs by those under 18 years of age; substantially reduce drug-related deaths; significantly increase the number of drug addicts successfully treated and substantially reduce drug-related crime, with money laundering and trafficking at the top of the list. as regards demand reduction, preventive measures and programmes for children and young people should address drug addiction in general, including alcoholism and smoking, rather than focusing exclusively on illicit drugs. training of professionals in the social, health, educational and judicial fields is essential for effective action. as regards supply reduction, the emergence of new synthetic drugs forces us to find ways of responding rapidly to the emergence of new substances and consumption trends. the establishment of voluntary monitoring mechanisms for new chemicals used in the illicit manufacture of synthetic drugs, as well as increased cooperation with the chemical industry, will be key priorities in this area. efforts to reduce the scale of money laundering must be intensified through the rapid adoption and implementation of the recently proposed amendments to the anti-money laundering directive. in line with the decisions taken at the tampere european council, priority should be given to the prevention of juvenile, urban and drug-related crime and to the progressive harmonisation of european legislation on illicit drug trafficking. in the past, member states and the commission have not given sufficient priority to the evaluation of anti-drug activities. that has to change. evaluation must become an integral part of the european approach. the commission has already started this evaluation and hopes to be able to go further in the future. the lisbon observatory can help by publishing guidelines for the evaluation of supply and demand reduction activities. the use of five harmonised key indicators - treatment demands by drug users, drug-related deaths, drug-related mortality and causes of death, incidence of drug-related infectious diseases, comparability of drug use surveys, public behaviour and attitudes towards drugs, and finally, comparability of overall estimates of the problem of drug use - plays an important role in this context. the adoption of the european union's drugs strategy for the first years of the second millennium does not mean that the debate is over. i believe that the next portuguese presidency will follow the european drugs strategy by presenting even more concrete priorities for the period 2000-04. we will also have the opportunity to work with the european institutions on the organisation of an interinstitutional conference to discuss the implementation of the european drugs strategy, if possible early next year. i hope that by then we will be able to assess the interpillar meeting suggested by the rapporteur. the commission's communication represents, in my view, a good starting point for a comprehensive, multidisciplinary and integrated european strategy to combat illicit drugs within the framework defined by the united nations general assembly in 1998. the lisbon observatory and europol in the hague are two important instruments which can make a significant contribution to our strategy. i am therefore convinced that we have the necessary means and will find the political will to tackle these new challenges in the context of the european drugs strategy for 2000-04.

the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, the commission has tabled a proposal for a regulation amending another community regulation, regulation (eec) no 1911/91, which established the special legal regime for the canary islands. regulation (eec) no 1911/91 is itself a regulation amending the status of these islands as defined by the act of accession of spain and portugal to the european communities of 1985. the act of accession of spain and portugal to the european communities - in article 25 and protocol no 2 annexed to that act - gave the canary islands a special status, characterised by the fact that the canary islands were not integrated into the common agricultural policy and, moreover, because they were not subject to the community customs union, the community tariff system and value added tax. in this way, the act of accession attempted to maintain, as far as possible, the special status which the canary islands had enjoyed within the spanish state since their incorporation into the crown of castile in the 15th century. this area was not subject to the ordinary taxation and, of course, to customs standards, due to the great distance separating it from the peninsular territory. the 1985 act of accession included an evolutionary clause - article 25 (4) - the purpose of which was to prevent the canary islands from being excluded from the european union as a result of the enlargement. i would say that canarian public opinion was, on the one hand, in favour of maintaining the specific features but, on the other hand, it did not want to remain on the margins of european construction. when the single act was adopted in 1986, it became necessary to amend this special scheme, which was done by regulation (eec) no 1911/91. this amendment introduces three or four very important changes: firstly, the canary islands are integrated into the common agricultural policy and the common fisheries policy; secondly, they are integrated into the community customs union and are therefore subject to the ordinary community customs tariffs; and thirdly, they are seeing disappear the forms of special taxation they used to enjoy, namely the island taxes - the so-called 'special tax licence scheme' - designed to protect local industry. in accordance with regulation (eec) no 1911/91, the canary islands' tax specificities were gradually dismantled and incorporated into the community's common system. but this has created disadvantages, because the problem of the canary islands, like other outermost regions - the azores, madeira and the french overseas departments - is that they are regions very far from the community territory, divided into small island territories, with very restricted markets, enormous transport problems and, in addition, difficulties arising, for example, from overcrowding, a very irregular rainfall and poor soils, which prevent the development of normal activities. this explains why spain has always recognised the specific features of the canary islands in the past. the dismantling of the canary islands' special tax arrangements for customs tariffs would threaten the dismantling of a number of small local industries - food, tobacco and small commercial industries - which would disappear if the small protection afforded by the canary islands' special taxes, namely the arbitrary production and import tax (apim), were to be completely abolished. the commission has been sympathetic and aware of all this, which is why it has begun to negotiate an adjustment of the apim in order to prevent the disappearance of this tax. there was also another element: the 1992 maastricht treaty already contained a declaration recognising the special situation of the outermost regions - the canary islands, the azores, madeira and the french overseas departments - and article 299 (2) of the ec treaty, as amended by the 1997 treaty of amsterdam, provides for a special regime for the outermost regions. the treaty of amsterdam is already in force. in accordance with the philosophy of the new regime for the outermost regions - which was also confirmed by the cologne european council, which asked the commission to present measures for the outermost regions by 31 december - the integration of these regions into the european union does not necessarily require tariff and fiscal harmonization at present, but allows for differentiated treatment, for example the maintenance of maritime concessions in the french overseas departments and special regimes in the azores and madeira. although the commission's proposal for a regulation began to be negotiated before the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam, the committee on legal affairs and the internal market - which approves the proposal for a regulation as a whole, since it is aimed at postponing the disarmament of canarian taxes and therefore has a protective function - believes that after the entry into force of article 299.2, the limitation of the special treatment should not simply be adjusted, but its elimination paralysed because, in the measures to be proposed by the commission for the outermost regions in accordance with article 299.2, which provides for special measures in the field of fiscal policy, it is foreseeable that the commission will have to allow a small rearmament so that the small local industries concerned are not harmed. as i said earlier, mr president, the legal affairs committee has unanimously approved the regulation, but it proposes a series of amendments to show that article 299.2, already in force, provides an additional basis for the commission's proposal for a regulation. we are not trying to go against the commission's regulation, which establishes an additional basis. this would justify what we might call a measure of restraint or suspension of the disarmament of customs tariffs. in the light of this reference to article 299.2 and the philosophy i am now setting out, the legal affairs committee has proposed a series of amendments to the annexes to the regulation so that we do not pursue the disarmament of customs tariffs in accordance with one of the concepts currently in force. the current protectionist structure of taxation should be maintained until the commission presents new proposals on tax policy. as the commissioner knows, a partnership meeting is being held in brussels next week, during which the commission will discuss proposals in this area with the governments of spain, france and portugal and with the governments of the autonomous regions and the european parliamentarians from these regions. i therefore think it is appropriate for the commission to approve or to agree with the proposals of parliament - the legal affairs committee - which are very reasonable and coincide with the philosophy of the commission, but reinforce it with reference to the new article 299.2, which provides for and allows the development of a special regime. it would not make much sense for us to proceed now to the total elimination of the system when it is possible that in a few months' time the commission will have to propose its rearmament. that is the philosophy, that is the problem, and i hope that this parliament will follow the recommendations of the legal affairs committee, that it will approve the regulation, but also the 19 amendments proposed unanimously by the committee mentioned above.

negotiated our country's accession to the european communities and in the successive treaties leading up to the amsterdam treaty, and the constant concern that this specific situation should always be taken into account, is reflected, as early as 1985, in special protocol no 2 to the act of accession of spain and portugal, in council regulation (eec) no 1911/91 which approved this protocol, and in paragraph 2 of article 299 of the ec treaty itself, which describes the peripheral regions of the union with a special reference to the canary islands and prescribes the flexibility necessary for the application of the general standards to specific and vulnerable cases such as the one we are dealing with here. it is precisely protocol no 2, to which i referred earlier, which, by adapting to the new law what had been only traditional formulae, establishes the apim, a modest customs duty by which certain products are taxed upon entry into the canary islands, many of them coming from peninsular spain itself and others from other states. a process is currently under way which will lead to negotiations between the spanish government and the commission with a view to amending regulation (eec) no 1911/91, which specifically regulates the apim in question. the concern that this change has aroused in the canary islands - and which we echo - has grown along with a certain distrust of the ability of my own government to understand the real importance and gravity of this problem and its willingness to deal with it in the aforementioned negotiation with the commission. there are, in fact, only three alternatives. the first is the radical abolition of the apim, which would have very negative consequences for a very large number of small and mediumsized industries in the islands, which, although they obtain low profit margins on their production, survive thanks to the fact that similar products from outside are precisely taxed and that it is, therefore, always profitable to continue their production in the canaries. the second alternative is less abrupt but, in the end, just as damaging. the aim would be to phase out the apim until it disappears completely after a few years, perhaps keeping it partially for a few articles. the third solution is the one proposed by professor medina and the one which, in our opinion, meets the needs and expectations of the canaries, the one which this parliament will probably vote on in a few moments. on the basis of the legal considerations of the ec treaty, we are calling for the continuation of the apim, virtually as it is at present, by consolidating it through the necessary reform of regulation (eec) no 1911/91. we hope that our parliament will rise to the occasion and not disappoint our fellow citizens ... - the next item is the report (a5-0065/1999) by mrs breyer, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on limit values for benzene and carbon monoxide in ambient air (com (98) 591 - c4-0135/1999 - 1998/0333 (cod)).
commission - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection and, of course, in particular the rapporteur, mrs breyer, for her excellent report. i also thank you for your excellent contribution to this debate. the proposal under consideration is the second to be submitted by the commission in the context of framework directive 96/62 on the assessment and management of air quality. it will set new limit values. these values are based on the most recent advice from the world health organisation. there are many areas where the commission can accept the constructive amendments proposed by the committee on the environment. we accept the amendments which bring this proposal into line with the final position on the first daughter directive on air quality 1999/30, adopted this year in april. we therefore accept amendments nos 1 and 6. i share the view of the committee on the environment that the most contentious point concerns the limit values for benzene and the timetables for reaching them. it is difficult to deal with the question of benzene, since there is no identifiable threshold value for effects. in principle, the commission can accept amendment no 2 which clarifies this point. we suggest a slight modification which respects the terminological norms, namely: 'considering that benzene is a genotoxic carcinogenic gene, for which there is no threshold value below which it would not constitute a risk to human health'. as regards the limit values, the commission considers that its proposal of an average annual concentration of 5 micrograms per m3 is well balanced. it will provide a high level of protection but, as a general rule, it should be applicable throughout the union over the next ten years. the commission cannot accept amendment no 20 setting the limit value at 4 micrograms per m3. however, it is clear that the limit values for carcinogens need to be constantly reviewed. the commission will prepare reports on benzene in 2004 as part of the newly integrated clean air programme. as the proposal makes clear, we will then consider the possibility of proposing a new limit value for the longer term. although the commission considers that its proposals are, in general, feasible by 2010, some uncertainties remain. this is largely due to the fact that there is no limit value for benzene and no consistent control within the union at present. however, it is clear that the ease with which problems can be solved depends to some extent on the climate. the commission has therefore asked the parliament and the council in article 3 (2) whether this should be taken into account. the commission, having listened to the discussions so far, believes that member states should be able to ask for longer periods to meet the limit values for benzene. the delay until 2010 would cause serious socioeconomic problems. it therefore does not accept amendment no 17 or the rest of amendment no 20. however, we accept that the conditions for obtaining a derogation should be made clearer and stricter. on balance, the commission considers that the extension can be limited to a maximum of five years. it therefore accepts most of amendment no 22, which we prefer to amendment no 5. however, it considers that it cannot support the temporary limit value of 10 micrograms per m3 without gathering information on its feasibility. the commission cannot accept this part of amendment no 22. amendment no 11 is linked to amendment no 22 and the commission accepts it partially. the commission does not accept the fact that amendment no 11 includes a requirement that a stricter limit value for benzene should be proposed in 2004. it is already clearly stated in the proposal that the purpose of this review will be to take account of the most recent scientific evidence and, if necessary, to further improve protection. we should leave these decisions on hold until we have all the scientific evidence. the commission can accept amendment no 10 which stresses the importance of considering the effects on sensitive populations. the commission agrees with the committee on the environment that indoor conditions have a significant impact on health but we do not think that this proposal offers us the means to tackle this problem. the subject is much broader and goes beyond benzene and carbon monoxide. it must therefore be considered in a broader context and, from a technical point of view, directive 96/62 defines ambient air as 'outside air' only. the commission cannot therefore accept amendments nos 3 and 12 or amendment no 18, which is partly linked to them. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the environment is not affected by pollution. the dissemination of high-quality and up-to-date information to the public is a key element of the new framework for improving air quality. the commission can accept the extract from amendment no 7 which aims to extend the list of means that member states could use to inform the public about air quality. however, it does not accept the part that states that member states must draw up lists of organisations which collect information and forward it to the commission. during the discussions on the first daughter directive it was decided that such lists would be too bureaucratic and might even be misleading. the commission accepts amendment no 8, which requires more information on carbon monoxide and considers that it improves its proposal. it can also accept amendment no 9 in part. annex 6, point ii, deals with data on pollution levels. these should be actively made available to the public in accordance with the aarhus convention. the documents referred to in annex 4, point 3, are however highly technical and potentially voluminous. they should be available on request but should not be actively disseminated. the commission agrees with the rapporteur that member states should take particular care to provide the public with information in all areas and with detailed timetables for reaching the limit values for benzene. therefore, we can accept amendment no 19 in principle. we propose that the following should be added to article 6 (2): 'member states shall pay particular attention to the dissemination of information to the public on concentrations, plans and programmes in the fields referred to in article 3 (2) '. the commission can also accept amendment no 4 in principle. however, we suggest that the words 'measurements' be replaced by the word 'concentration', which will demonstrate the fact that information must be disseminated whether it has been obtained by measurements or by any other method. ensuring that member states assess air quality in a consistent and comparable way is a third objective of both the air quality framework directive and this proposal. however, the commission does not accept amendment no 13. the amendment, as drafted, raises unnecessary technical problems. member states will have to inform the commission of the measurement methods, as well as the number and location of the measuring stations each year. this is already part of the general reporting requirements of council directive 96/62 and council decision 97/101 on the mutual exchange of air quality information. the commission also rejects amendment no 14. it is not compatible with the decisions contained in the first daughter directive on air quality. according to the general technical advice, taking measurements, with regard to the annual mean limit values, close to the façade lines better reflects the exposure of the population. the commission can accept amendment no 15 in part. it considers that this proposal should be harmonised with directive 1999/30 by inserting the following sentence: in areas or agglomerations with more than one measuring station, at least one station must be located close to traffic and at least one must be oriented towards an urban context. however, i think that the additional requirement that at least half of the stations should be traffic-centric is excessive. in conclusion, the commission agrees with the intention of amendments nos 16 and 21. directive 96/62 allows the use of random measures if it can be shown that they are sufficiently precise. these amendments seek to describe what this means for benzene. amendment no 16 follows closely the first daughter directive. the commission considers, however, that in the case of the annual average limit value for benzene, it is possible to require a higher standard of accuracy, equal to that established for continuous checks. it therefore prefers amendment no 21 to amendment no 16. in conclusion, i hope that it will be possible to reach agreement on this proposal in the short term. at present there are no community limit values for benzene and carbon monoxide. the adoption of such legislation is essential to ensure that adequate controls can be carried out and that member states can identify areas of concern. this is a crucial factor in ensuring that public health is properly protected within the union. i would like to make one last comment to mr goodwill on enlargement because you make a very good point. at the moment it is difficult to obtain good quality information and measures on this from the candidate countries. we must follow this matter very closely. we are already working with the candidate countries and have already drawn up review reports, as you know. so we have to work a lot with the candidate countries and you raise an important point. this should be added to the list of tasks that we have to accomplish from now on. i thank you for that and i thank you for the debate.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0064/1999) by mrs gonzález álvarez, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the common position of the council with a view to adopting a european parliament and council decision establishing a programme for the monitoring of the average specific emissions of co2 from new passenger cars (com (98) 348 - c5-0041/1999 - 1998/0202 (cod)).
the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, this is the second reading, as the president said, of a common position of the council on the reduction of co2 emissions from new vehicles. it should be remembered that this second reading is an attempt to achieve the kyoto targets, which were subsequently agreed in bonn, for greenhouse gas emissions, targets which still seem modest to us. if we take into account the report of the european environment agency, which said that we had to reduce emissions by 30%, the targets proposed to us are modest. in any case, this common position, which aims to prevent new cars from emitting more and more co2, seems to us to be a good one. at first reading, 45 amendments were tabled in the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy and they were approved by a large majority. of these 45 amendments, 29 were approved in plenary and the council should be thanked for having taken up a large number of these 29 amendments in the common position. but in the end we tabled 10 amendments again. they were approved, with one abstention, by over 40 votes in favour in the committee on the environment. these are amendments which take up some of the issues which seemed important to the majority of the committee on the environment at first reading. some simply take up changes in terms, such as amendment no 1, which says that we must not just stabilise greenhouse gas emissions, in this case co2, we must reduce them. in amendment no 2 we submit to monitoring on an objective basis. we have made a change on a proposal from the commission. in amendment no 3 we are talking about the legal framework that should be prepared in the event that voluntary agreements fail. i would like to point out that parliament in general, and the committee on the environment in particular, is sceptical about the actual results of voluntary agreements. that is why we are submitting the presentation of a legal framework. we are also talking about tax incentives and the inclusion of commercial vehicles, which should not be left out of the proposal because they emit a significant amount of co2. we propose a change in the way we collect data, in case it is found that it has not produced results over a given period. the council's common position itself mentions that the member states have different proposals for collecting data. we also ask for a report on the operation of this method in december 2002. we have also made a small change here on the commission's proposal. we wanted to have this report by june 2002 and we put off december to give a little more time. we also want the report that the commission is to present to the council and the european parliament to analyse whether the possible reduction in co2 emissions is due to technical measures by industry or to consumer habits. amendment no 10, which the commission and the council are proposing to adopt, concerns the weight and size of cars. we are grateful to the council and the commission for accepting certain amendments. but we feel we must insist on some of the 10 amendments which we are putting back here because they were actually approved almost unanimously, with one abstention, in the committee on the environment. the commission and council representatives themselves have said that they are still analysing some of them, for example the one on tax incentives and the inclusion of commercial vehicles. we therefore believe that these amendments in any case only support the commission and council's study process on tax incentives or commercial vehicles. we believe that these are amendments which the commission and the council can easily accept. we are well aware of the difficulty the council has in convincing the 15 member states of a proposal with such characteristics, but it must be said that, having consulted practically all the groups, they insist that we must retain these amendments and i am defending the environment committee's proposal here.
commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the committee on the environment, and in particular the rapporteur, mrs gonzález álvarez, for the diligence with which she has dealt with this matter. it is in the interest of all parties that this decision be taken without further delay, so that we can implement objective monitoring of the environmental agreements which have been concluded with the automobile industry. mrs gonzález álvarez indicated in her recommendation that the common position contained many of the views expressed by the european parliament at first reading. as mrs schleicher said, mrs flemming said that she could accept the common position without further amendments. we must be aware that the only way for this decision to come into force before the end of the year is for us to adopt the common position as it stands. otherwise, the data compilation will be delayed by a full year. as regards the amendments which have been tabled, we fully support three which could improve the common position, namely amendments 3, part 1, and amendments 7 and 10. we also support in principle a number of other proposals. these are amendments nos 2 and 4, part two, and proposal 9, although we believe that they should be reworded. i should like to briefly explain the reasons for the commission's position. i would first like to comment on amendment no 2 which seeks to extend the decision to other motor vehicles. following a request made by the european parliament at first reading, the commission is now taking the first steps to include fuel consumption and carbon dioxide emissions of light commercial vehicles in the type-approval legislation: these are therefore vehicles of category m1. the commission will then examine whether it is possible to reduce the carbon dioxide emissions from these vehicles. the commission agrees with parliament that it is these types of vehicles that are the most important to be dealt with. therefore, there are currently no plans to study the possibility of including other types of vehicles, mainly because it is hoped that they, for example trucks, can achieve high fuel efficiency, or because they are vehicles (for example two-wheelers) that contribute only a small share of carbon dioxide emissions at local level. the commission intends to take this into account and to reword the proposed text as follows: 'the commission is considering the possibility of submitting reasonable proposals to harmonize the procedures for measuring specific emissions of carbon dioxide emitted by vehicles of category m1 in accordance with annex iii to directive 70/156. " as regards the second part of amendment no 4, which relates to the other parts of the strategy on co2 emitted by vehicles, we consider that the first point almost entirely coincides with reason no 6 of the common position. we cannot accept this part of the amendment, because it is necessary to refer to the community target of 120 g/km. however, the 2010 deadline for achieving this objective is not mentioned in the european parliament's amendment. the second part of the reasoning refers to the second and third pillars for the strategy to be adopted on carbon dioxide emissions from motor vehicles, opting in this case for consumer information and the application of fiscal measures. the consumer information directive was accepted by the european parliament at second reading on 4 november this year and can therefore be considered as adopted. it is in line with the common position. so there is no reason to go back on this. since tax measures are an important part of the strategy, it might be useful to include a wording on this. since the commission is already considering the possibility of creating a reference framework, it would be good if this situation were clearly set out in the grounds. the commission therefore proposes the following: 'the commission is studying the possibilities of establishing a reference framework for tax measures which could encourage the use of fuel-efficient passenger cars'. as regards amendment no 9 on the content of the annual report, the rapporteur would like to add a new article which would define more clearly the content of the report, namely, inter alia, an analysis of the relationship between the evolution of carbon dioxide emissions and the efforts made by the car manufacturers, or other factors which fall within the scope of our strategy. it is important to carry out such an analysis to determine whether the manufacturers are actually undertaking the tasks to which they have committed themselves under the environmental agreement. this applies, for example, to the interim objectives set for the year 2003 and, of course, also to the final objectives set for 2008. however, this requires considerable efforts in terms of analytical methods and technical studies and intensive exchanges with manufacturers. it will also take several years before we can see whether any significant change has taken place. the commission will therefore in all likelihood only undertake the first evaluations once the deadlines for the intermediate and final objectives have expired. this fact should be reflected in the text of the decision. we therefore propose to reformulate it as follows: 'the reports for the years when the intermediate and final targets must have been met must indicate whether the reductions have been achieved as a result of technical measures applied by the manufacturers or whether they are due to other causes such as a change in consumer behaviour. " we find it difficult to accept the remaining amendments, namely 1, 3, part two, 4, part one, 5, 6 and 8, which do not improve or clarify the text. finally, i should like to say a few words about amendment no 3, part two. it recommends that the commission should draw up a legal framework for environmental agreements. i would like to stress that the question of the involvement of the european parliament in the implementation of these agreements is, in my view, a decisive one. as i explained in the plenary on 3 november, i do not intend to put forward any new proposals for agreements in this area until parliament's role has been defined. that is why we are currently working on a general document on environmental agreements, their legal framework and the corresponding institutional procedures. with regard to the agreements on co2 emissions from passenger cars which have already been concluded or are in the process of being concluded, the commission has repeatedly stressed that the legislation on emission thresholds would be subject to monitoring if the automotive industry does not meet its commitments. however, it would be inappropriate to make technical preparations for such legislation in advance. it would send the wrong message to the industry. in conclusion, i should like to express my satisfaction that the common position has been received so positively by the rapporteur and the committee on the environment. i now hope for the support of the house so that the decision can be taken as quickly as possible. we will then be able to monitor in sufficient detail the implementation of the environmental agreements concluded with the automobile industry. if the plenary considers it necessary to table further amendments, the commission will be prepared to accept them in a number of cases, either as such or in principle.
- thank you very much, commissioner, for the detailed reply you gave to the rapporteur and to the speakers who took part in this debate. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 11 a.m.

- the next item is the report (a5­0072/1999) by mr pesälä, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a council directive on the marketing of forest reproductive material (com (99) 188 - c5­0128/1999 - 1999/0092 (cns)).
- (es) mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we must welcome this proposal for a directive for a number of reasons, not least because it has broadened its scope. today, it is considering timber production but also other forestry objectives, such as cork and the protection of genetic resources. we should also welcome the fact that it identifies different categories, and that it promotes the protective nature of reforestation and not just the production of wood. it assumes the greatest variability from the genetic point of view, thus guaranteeing adaptation. the proposal largely reflects the different needs of the member states, without losing sight of the principle of subsidiarity. the accession of the nordic and mediterranean countries to the european union was the main reason for updating the directive, which is currently in force and regulates the marketing of seeds and forestry plants, and which has not been substantially amended since 1975. the text of the directive corresponds in its basic aspects - objective, number of categories, definitions of basic material, etc. - to the other major system for the marketing of forest reproductive material at world level, that of the oecd. in recent years work has been undertaken to update this system and a revised text is already available and is being approved by the council. the correspondence between the two texts can only facilitate the marketing of these materials. i also want to and must congratulate mr pesälä on his report. i agree with him that the date for the directive to enter into force cannot be 1 january 2000, the deadline must be extended by at least three years to give member states time to adapt to the directive. other amendments tabled by other members, such as those tabled by mrs schierhuber, must also be welcomed, including the one aimed at strengthening the control of the flow of goods through an official certificate of origin. but there is one important point which we must take into account and that is that in the explanatory statement it is specified that the external quality of the materials was guaranteed. however, annex vii (d) deals with it in a very generic way. this is not a trivial matter. the quality of the plant is essential in the mediterranean basin, where reforestation is carried out under very difficult conditions. experience has shown that from certain sizes the plant has no chance of surviving in an environment, as is the case in many parts of southern europe where the drought conditions are very extreme. to facilitate root establishment, plants grown in containers with good root systems are used, whereas in other countries bare roots are successfully used. the outer quality of the plant has a significant impact, not only on the percentage of plants that survive, which can go from 85% to 20%, but also on future development in the extremely harsh conditions of their transplantation in this climate. the external quality is one of the factors that determines the quality of wood in the future. therefore, the lack of regulation of the outer quality of the plant can cause very serious problems, since it allows plants of all sizes to appear on the market. please note that some member states already have legal instruments for regulation. the environment of the whole of europe has an interest in plantings being carried out correctly and a good part of them not failing. the plants must be suitable, they must be adaptable, because unfortunately in many parts of the european union you cannot plant what you want but what you can. in order to ensure that this unresolved problem is adequately addressed in the text of the proposal, the council is adopting by common accord the inclusion of a new point 7 which sets out the external characteristics which must be possessed by the forest species best adapted to the difficult soil and climatic conditions of the mediterranean regions of the community for their marketing. i would like to applaud and encourage this solution, which i hope the european commission will support.
commission - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the committee on agriculture and rural development and, of course, its rapporteur, mr pesälä, for the very positive marketing of forest reproductive material, in order to take account of the accession of new member states since 1975, the internal market and scientific progress. twenty-two amendments were proposed. commission proposal fully recognises the specificity of the conditions of certain member states or parts of them, and the text expressly reflects this position. i come now to amendment no 7. the commission says this in the first part of article 5 (2) (b): the procedures ensuring the equivalence of the environmental risk assessment and other relevant elements with those laid down in council the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, commissioner, regulation (ec) no 2201/96 provided for aid to the tomato processing industry to compensate for the difference in the cost of community raw materials compared with the world market. this aid was granted on the basis of an overall eu quota of almost 7 million tonnes, broken down over five years by product group (peeled tomatoes, concentrates and other products). each year there is a breakdown within each group by member state of the average minimum price observed during the three marketing years preceding the marketing year for which the quotas are allocated. the same regulation, for the 1997-98 and 1998-99 marketing years, provides for a distribution of quotas which was slightly modified in 1997, as one group was transferred to another. from that date onwards, for the following marketing year, the allocation shall be made on the basis of the quantities which have respected the minimum price during the last three marketing years, as provided for in article 6 (4) of that regulation. the proposal does not merely change the regulation, it requires the agreement of the council of ministers. this is really an exception to the regulation because portugal failed to reach the quota allocated to it in the 1997/98 marketing year because of what is said to be bad weather conditions. it is proposed that portugal be allocated an additional quantity of 83 468 tonnes for the 1999-2000 marketing year and, for the 2001 marketing year, the difference between the quota calculated on the basis of the quantities actually processed in 1997-98 and 884 592 tonnes. no economic impact will be recorded by the other member states, since this quota increase granted to portugal will be the subject of an ad hoc budget. nevertheless, this agreement by the council of ministers has caused considerable unease among producers in other countries - specifically in spain, italy and greece - which are really very competitive in the processing and production of tomatoes. as the president knows, protesters have even gathered outside the ministry of agriculture in spain to protest against what they consider to be a free gift to portugal. the transition from a quota system to a threshold system would provide a fairer, clearer and more transparent form of contracting and allocation. in a way, this can satisfy producers in countries that are more competitive. the committee on agriculture and rural development and this parliament are in no way seeking that portugal should benefit from this additional quota in order to adapt and become more competitive in its tomato production, but it would be an important opportunity to move from the quota system to the guarantee thresholds per member state. and that is the point of the amendments i have tabled to this proposal for a regulation. two amendments concern the recitals, where it is considered that the processing aid formula is really important, that the quota is insufficient and that the commission will present, before the start of the next marketing year, a proposal to change from a quota system to a threshold system. i hope the commission will accept it.

the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, the current common organization of the market has shown signs of weakness since it was no longer able to meet the new challenges of a highly globalised and competitive market, such as that for fishery products, in a european union which is highly dependent on imports. parliament had repeatedly pointed out this imbalance and called for far-reaching changes. today we are finally discussing the report of the committee on fisheries on a proposal for a regulation which does not propose a simple reform of the com but a new regulation. i would like to see it as fruitful and responsible as the debate we had in the committee on fisheries, because this report, which i ask for approval, is the fruit of a much sought-after compromise between the various political groups and the various sectoral and national interests. as rapporteur, i think it is fair to say that the commission's original proposal was a great improvement on the current cmo, in particular because it reinforced the fundamental role that producer organisations play in the marketing of products and gave them more and better mechanisms for proper operation, more responsible fishing and marketing. our committee, however, had to amend the text of the proposal in two very important respects, and in both cases it did so by means of the compromises to which i have referred earlier. it has achieved the former by introducing aquaculture products and seafood for which no marketing aid was provided, whereas these are two subsectors which, like fisheries, must be fully included in a system whose objective is to match supply to demand and whereas, as in the case of aquaculture, these two sectors are in the process of development and must rely on good production planning from the outset in order to avoid, as far as possible, crises such as those periodically suffered by salmon producers, for example. the other aspect, which has been modified, is even more serious because, if, as i said at the beginning of my speech, this is the kind of regulation for which it would be appropriate to propose, without any haste, in the import sector, the replacement of the tariff quota system by a system of suspension of customs duties for an indefinite period, the commission has not only acted without thinking but has shown great frivolity and irresponsibility. the committee on fisheries does not oppose the system of suspension of customs duties. i want to make this very clear. but this system, which is in fact a voluntary tariff disarmament, requires absolute certainty that community firms producing and marketing the same products will not be put at risk. the commission proposal cited several products for which there is community production and substantial community production, as would seem to be demonstrated by the study currently being drawn up at the request of the council and given the lack of justification for the commission's figures. this study establishes deficit levels of between 1 500 and 3 000 tonnes for some of these products - tuna nets, for example. in other words, the commission was preparing to smother, cheerfully and without comparing the data at its disposal, a community sector which provides thousands of jobs, and its development aid schemes for the gsp countries and acp countries, by requiring real imports of less than 3 000 tonnes, which can be covered perfectly well by the present system of customs quotas. although it was particularly difficult to reach a compromise in our committee on this point, the facts seem to confirm our view since, following the political agreement reached at the last council of ministers, both tuna and herring nets are being removed from the system of suspension of customs duties, in addition to a series of amendments concerning other products in annex v. i therefore think that the commission proposal was not well thought out, that it was dangerous and we welcome the council amendment, which is in addition to our own and is to provide for more flexible compensation for withdrawals. i therefore believe that, by means of these two major amendments which have been tabled in committee along with others, such as greater precision in labelling and consumer information, parliament is helping to prevent a text - which i believe has some interesting points, as i have already said - from being unrealistic in its application and therefore i ask you all to approve this report. mr president, i would just like to thank all the members who have helped to achieve this compromise, to thank them for their good work and cooperation, and i would ask again for the report to be adopted. i thank you and i also congratulate mr gallagher on his report.

commission. - thank you, madam president, for inviting me to speak today on the two commission proposals. as you know, my colleague mr fischler is in seattle at the moment and has asked me to take his place. the first is the reform of the common organisation of the market in fishery and aquaculture products. the commission welcomes the report of the european parliament's committee on fisheries and in particular the detailed analysis by its rapporteur, mrs fraga estévez, who makes a valuable contribution to the debate. the work of this committee, which met for the last time on this subject on the same day as the fisheries council on 22 november, has directly informed the council's discussions in this area. as you know, the council has reached a broad consensus. mr fischler, for his part, only provisionally accepted this consensus, telling the ministers that he could only give his consent to a final decision after considering the opinion of the european parliament. i listened with interest to the speeches made today and i think they illustrate well the diversity of the fisheries market across the union and therefore underline the need for us to take these elements into account. we now have to look at the proposal and the opinion of the parliament from the point of view of their impact on all the parties concerned and not just on the producers. i would like to stress the importance of this reform being applied throughout the fishing chain and thus encouraging market integration. the main change in the commission's proposal is that the common organisation of the market will now cover consumers as well as the whole fisheries industry. this commission proposal is good for consumers, good for producers, good for the processing industry, and i will tell you why. as far as consumers are concerned, the commission proposal provides that essential information on the product will be provided. the consumer will know what kind of fish he is buying, how it was produced and where it came from. given the importance of traceability in all its aspects in the food sector, in particular in terms of food safety, these provisions will provide consumers with reassurance and allow them to make better informed purchasing decisions. i am pleased to note, madam president, that the european parliament agrees with this. however, the origin of the fishing vessel is not of direct interest to consumers and its mention could be perceived as distorting trade with third countries. for producers, the commission's proposal aims to reorient the incentives provided by the common organisation of the market to encourage better supply planning. the commission has strengthened the role of producer organisations by proposing a new mechanism that encourages producers to plan their activities in order to improve the balance between supply and demand. better planning should lead to a reduction in withdrawals and thus avoid waste. the commission can accept the general thrust of parliament's amendment in this area concerning the inclusion of producer organisations of certain aquaculture species in the scope of operational programmes. we also recognise that some of the benefits of better planning can also be applied to the aquaculture sector. while we support the idea of financial support for these programmes, we believe that this support should be granted on a temporary basis and should not be linked to the value of production because of the difficulties that could arise from the rules of world trade. the second aspect of the changes affecting producers concerns the level of community support in the form of intervention. the commission considers that a high level of withdrawals is not justified given the scarcity of fishery resources both inside and outside community waters. if we are to strive for sustainability in the fishing industry, we must not encourage the destruction of our resources. the intervention should become a safety net for fishermen, which would be used only rarely. the commission is of the opinion that we should reduce permanent withdrawals as much as possible and switch to support for more active fishermen's organisations, better adapted to the needs of the market. the european parliament's amendments in this area advocate a less radical reduction in the quantities eligible for support and in the financial assistance for withdrawal, which is in line with the emerging consensus among member states in the council. the commission will therefore not stand in the way of an agreement, but would be reluctant to accept the full amount of the proposed increases in intervention. as far as the processing industry is concerned, the situation with regard to trade with third countries is of paramount importance. our manufacturing industry must be able to source raw materials at world market prices to be competitive. otherwise we risk exporting jobs outside the community to countries which can easily obtain commodities at competitive prices. there are very different views on the form of the tariff duties to be applied to most sensitive species: tuna, herring and cod. i admit there are no easy answers. however, the parliament's recommendation to set a set of criteria for future suspensions, instead of a decision on tariff suspensions under the common market organisation, does not solve the problem. we must now create a more stable situation for the manufacturing industry. in its approach, the commission mainly applies the criterion that imported products must be raw materials for the processing industry for which the volume of community production is insufficient. it is clear that the short and longterm prospects for the supply of white fish are worrying and that the community cannot afford to penalise its processing industry and let third countries create the added value provided by the industry. to conclude this first proposal, madam president, the analyses of the european parliament and the commission converge on certain key points of the reform, in particular on the need to strengthen the role of producer organisations in the fisheries and aquaculture sector and to improve the information provided to consumers. on the intervention side, the commission cannot go as far as the european parliament would like by relaxing the new discipline on pensions, as it considers this position to be essential in the context of our efforts to conserve our resources. as regards trade with third countries, where we have a different approach from the european parliament, the commission is of the opinion that this is an important structural problem in the european market which warrants immediate action to save jobs in the processing sector. i now turn to the second commission proposal, madam president, and i would like to thank its rapporteur, mr gallagher, for his report. the proposal amends for the third time regulation (ec) no 850/98 of 30 march 1998 and aims to improve the conservation of fishery resources by adopting technical measures that will better protect juveniles of marine organisms. the proposed scheme is based on a number of new elements which the commission was only able to collect after the adoption of this regulation. this will enhance the protection of adult herring and juveniles, while improving the protection of marine mammals. the commission proposal is supported by the relevant scientific organisations such as the international commission for the exploration of the sea and the scientific, technical and economic committee for fisheries. the commission welcomes the fact that the committee on fisheries has adopted mr gallagher's report, which approves the commission's proposal.
