the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, i have the honour to present this report on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, which has appointed me as institutional rapporteur. this report on the verification of credentials has a rationale and derives its legal basis from article 11 of the act concerning the election of the representatives of the european parliament annexed to the council decision of 20 september 1976. in accordance with this legal basis, it is the european parliament which checks the credentials of members until the uniform electoral procedure enters into force. therefore, this report on the verification of credentials refers to the results of the fifth elections to the european parliament held from 10 to 13 june 1999 and is based on the official communications from the various member states on the overall electoral results, including the names of the possible substitutes and their ranking as a result of the vote. in accordance with rule 7 (5) of our rules of procedure, every member of parliament is entitled to sit in parliament and on its bodies even if his credentials have not been verified or a decision on a possible challenge has not been taken. in other words, until this report is approved by an overwhelming majority, i hope, in the plenary tomorrow, all of us, all the members elected for the fifth parliament, will have exercised our mandate fully and without restriction. the rules also provide that if an elected member leaves parliament before this report has been approved in plenary, the vacancy and the appeal against it will be examined, in accordance with rule 8 of our rules of procedure and the relevant provisions of the act of 20 september 1976, in a separate procedure, independent of this report and to be held in due course. therefore, this report refers only to the obtaining of the mandate under the fifth direct elections to the european parliament. the competent national authorities of 14 member states sent their official notifications on 20 june 1999. in the case of the grand duchy of luxembourg, there was a delay in the appointment of the elected candidates due to the fact that the elections to the european parliament were held simultaneously with a national legislative vote. in these elections some candidates were vying for seats in the european parliament and the national parliament, and some candidates were potential members of the future luxembourg government, which, according to article 6 (1) of the act of 20 september 1976, is incompatible with the status of member of the european parliament. since the formation of the luxembourg government was delayed until the beginning of august, the mandate of viviane reding, now commissioner, could only be effective by virtue of the communication from the competent luxembourg authorities on 7 august. mrs reding's resignation will also be the subject of a separate report as i announced earlier. secondly, article 7 (2) of our rules the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, two years after the negative result of the referendum in switzerland on its integration into the european economic area, the council authorized the commission to negotiate bilateral agreements with that country in the areas it considered necessary. the draft regulation which is now before parliament for approval completes one of the agreements reached, namely an agreement on the carriage of goods and passengers by rail and road. under this agreement, switzerland authorizes a maximum number of community heavy goods vehicles of more than 28 tonnes to cross swiss territory until 2005, when switzerland, by adapting its legislation to that of the community, will no longer require a permit for lorries weighing less than 40 tonnes. the commission has also proposed that the commission should be given the power to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 290 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. for the year 2000, 250 000 full load driving licences for trucks over 28 tonnes registered in the european union were obtained. from 2001 onwards, licences will be issued for lorries of 34 tonnes, with transit liberalized for heavy goods vehicles of 28 to 34 tonnes. the quota will be 300 000 licences per year for 2001 and 2002 and 400 000 per year for 2003 and 2004. the number of trucks that can be used empty is fixed at 220 000. this regulation - excellent in my view - proposes a system for allocating these licences among the 15 community countries. each of them will be allocated 1 500 licences per year, the rest being distributed according to the actual or theoretical figures for bilateral traffic and transit. i have to express reservations about two negative aspects. on the one hand, this proposal is being debated and voted on by this parliament before we know the general agreement with switzerland, so we are being asked to approve part of it without knowing the whole. on the other hand, we lack definitive and complete statistics on the current flow of goods between switzerland and the european union although this study is about to be completed, providing in the regulation itself that in the year 2000 the current distribution figures may be changed in the event that the actual data deviate significantly from those forecast today. in both cases, i consider that our desire that this regulation, which must be adopted by the codecision procedure, may enter into force on the same day as the agreement, is sufficient to explain our eagerness. i fully agree with the substantive question, namely the proposed method of calculating the allocation of the number of licences between the various member states, and that in the circumstances mentioned it is the most objective, rigorous and fair method possible. the regulation also provides, as i have said, for an annual system of redistribution of unused licences. it is to be hoped that each member state will in turn allocate the licences it has been granted to its carriers according to the same objective criteria. i'll give you some figures to summarize. applying the proposed method, the distribution of the 1 650 000 full load driving licences over the five years would be as follows: approximately 36% for germany, 20.5% for italy, 15.5% for france, 7.8% for the netherlands, 6.6% for belgium, 3.8% for austria and the remaining 10% would be distributed among the other nine member states. mr president, some amendments from the two parliamentary committees which debated the draft improve certain details and contribute to the general fairness of the regulation or to the ease of its administration. i think it is essential that, as the committee on transport has decided by vote, the minimum allocation of 1 500 licences per member state proposed by the commission be maintained. i should like to remind you that this is a very modest figure, equivalent to two trips a day for each country, and that the sum of all these automatic allocation permits over the five years does not even reach 7% of the total. i would like to end by emphasizing once again the initial quality of the project. i congratulate the commission on this and ask my distinguished colleagues to approve this draft regulation.

mr bouwman. - (da) i am not sure that the commissioner has been able to answer the question. the commission would point out to the honourable member that it has opened three infringement procedures in this respect. the procedure concerning autostrade s.p.a. could have a positive outcome, since the italian authorities have shown a willingness to work in agreement with the commission and have taken steps to privatise the company. in view of the important consequences that this case may have, the commission will continue to follow the procedure and the case will not be closed until the commission is sure that the principles of transparency and equal treatment are respected. as regards the other concessions, the commission has opened two infringement proceedings and is examining the related issues. given their economic, political and social importance, these matters will also be discussed at a very short meeting with the italian authorities. in order to tackle this general problem in a more structural way, the commission has also recently started a horizontal survey of the current situation in all member states to identify community problems and problems arising in certain member states only. if this investigation reveals possible infringements, the commission will take further steps to address these problems. the new infrastructure investments planned by italy are not necessarily in contradiction with the transport policy of the european union. although member states are responsible for decisions on such investments, the commission is of the opinion that they must be based on the positive outcome of a comprehensive analysis of the benefits and social costs.

- question no 36 is therefore inadmissible in the absence of its author. i call question no 37 by mr juan naranjo escobar (h-0760/99): subject: quality of education and programmes in june 1998, the conference of ministers of education of the eu and other candidate countries in prague set the objective of defining a set of data for evaluating the different national education systems. the commission informed the council on 26 november that the ad hoc committee of experts had already drawn up a second provisional document on data and reference levels, on the basis of which the first european report on the quality of education will be presented at the next conference, to be held in bucharest in june 2000. in view of the state of progress of the work and the importance which the council attaches to cooperation between states in developing the quality of education as an instrument for improving the economy and employment, does the commission consider it appropriate to set up a standing committee of experts from the eu and other candidate countries on the quality of education? does the commission think that, in accordance with the first paragraph of article 149 of the treaty of amsterdam, this committee of experts could be asked to draw up criteria or recommendations for the establishment of a parallel common curriculum for all school systems at the level of the first years of primary education? second part
as the honourable member who asked this question will no doubt be aware, political cooperation between the member states in the field of the quality of education has been strengthened in recent years. the recommendation on quality in higher education adopted in september 1998 and another proposal for a recommendation on quality assessment in education show that we believe it is important to have a debate on the quality of education at european level. at the council of education ministers on 26 november, the issue was given further prominence by the adoption of a resolution on a revised agenda, making it one of the priorities for the coming years. following the conference of european ministers of education in prague in june 1998, a study committee on quality indicators was set up. this committee includes representatives from 26 european countries; the commission has drawn up progress reports for the ministers, one in june and one in october this year. the first european report on the quality of education will be presented to the council of education ministers, the conference of european ministers of education, to be held in bucharest in june 2000, and the european parliament. in the light of the discussions on the report, the commission will make proposals on how to deal with the indicators and quality criteria in the context of the revised agenda and the annual conference of ministers of education. the current study committee has proved to be an important forum for discussion; it is the site of many exchanges of information and experience on the quality of education between the member states and the candidate countries. the commission intends to propose that it be maintained. the european work on indicators and criteria serves as a basis for discussions on differences in outcomes between education systems and the reasons for these differences. the factors involved, such as curricula, teacher training, resources, evaluation and others, are discussed within the study committee on quality indicators and at ministerial level. the countries participating in the work of the study committee benefit from the exchange of information and experience on these various subjects. the commission welcomes the active participation of the european parliament in the debate on the quality of education and, in particular, in the forthcoming debate on the indicators and criteria for the quality of education.

- question no 38 by maría izquierdo rojo (h-0728/99) subject: machismo in the administration since the problem of the under-representation of women and their exclusion from senior positions cannot be solved by the presence of well-intentioned male directors, what measures will the commission propose to remedy the current situation, namely the fact that 90% of the posts in question are occupied by men?
commission -the commission agrees with the honourable member that women are still underrepresented at the top levels of the administration within the commission, as in other institutions. i would say to you, however, madam president, with all due respect, that it is wrong to say that women are excluded from these posts, just as it is unfair to accuse the commission of machismo. since 1988, the commission has adopted three action programmes to promote positive initiatives and equal opportunities within its services. particular attention was paid to the increase in the proportion of women in managerial and middle management positions. in 1996, an evaluation of the impact of the first two action programmes on equal opportunities in the commission revealed that the situation of women in category a and in managerial positions had changed considerably, particularly following the implementation of the annual targets set by the commission. while women accounted for 11.5% of the a-category workforce in 1992, they accounted for 19.3% in september this year. in 1992, women occupied approximately 2% of a2 posts, i.e. management posts, compared with 11% in september of this year. - question no 48 by mr sebastiano musumeci (h-0677/99): the commission has not yet decided whether to grant a discharge to the council. the court of justice has held that the organisation of games of chance is an economic activity of provision of services falling within the scope of the ec treaty, stating that the provisions of the member states relating to the authorisation of the opening of gambling houses must be proportionate to the objectives pursued and non-discriminatory (schindler c-275/92). the italian government requires that the favourable effects which the activities in question are likely to have on tourism and the seriousness of the applicant be demonstrated without defining criteria for this purpose, which leaves a large margin of discretion in the adoption of decisions. all the licences issued to date in italy have allowed the opening of only four casinos (compared with 119 in the united kingdom and about 102 in germany), all located in northern italy, which is a clear discrimination against objective 1 regions which could benefit greatly from the opening of gambling houses in terms of both tourist revenue and economic expansion. does the commission not consider that the italian government's attitude constitutes a breach of the community provisions on non-discrimination and free competition, in particular articles 12 to 86 of the treaty?
commission - (it) mr musumeci, i can only repeat what i have just said. the situation of gambling houses varies from one member state to another. the court confirmed that the member states have a decisionmaking power in this area. moreover, as regards the point you have made about the distribution of gambling establishments within the territory of a state, the competition rules and the principle of non-discrimination do not require member states to take account of regional aspects when they grant gambling establishments licences or other authorizations to organise games of chance. the competition rules do not preclude the criteria which a member state may use, so these rules cannot lead us to consider the decision taken by a member state as to the distribution of these gambling houses on its territory as arbitrary and therefore in breach of the competition rules.
- question no 49 by mr eduard beysen (h-0684/99): purpose: to be published in accordance with article 5 of council regulation (eec) no 19/65/eec of 2 march 1965 has the commission taken account of the specific nature and diversity of the horeka sector in belgium, which is renowned for its pleasant variety of coffees offering innumerable varieties of beer, and of the consequences which the implementation of the above-mentioned regulation will have, particularly for the small coffee growers who will be affected? in the absence of brewery contracts, the large market share holders will no longer invest in the coffee shops where they sell their products but will spend the money thus freed on mass advertising in order to strengthen their position. the result will obviously be a fierce price war, which will affect not only small breweries but also coffee producers. is the commission aware that market leaders not only sell their products but often add financial support (interest-bearing loans), equipment (installation of beer pumps, furniture, glasses, etc.) and technical support (refrigerators)? that means he's going to ask questions about the sale of beer in belgium according to these cabalistic figures. the commissioner has the floor.
the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. i think i understand what mr beysen is asking. the commission is aware that breweries often offer financial, material and technical support to the owners of coffee shops. the commission does not share the concern expressed by the honourable member that the new policy proposed on vertical restraints is likely to harm belgian breweries or the hotel and catering sector. on the contrary, effective competition will ensure that consumers are well served in terms of the number of bars and the variety of beer on offer. first, the proposed block exemption exempts beer supply contracts containing a non-competition clause, contracts between beer producers with a market share of less than 30% and owners of bars or public establishments. for belgian breweries, this means that all of them, with the exception of interbrew, will be able to continue to operate on the basis of the current distribution agreements. furthermore, the proposed generalised block exemption gives these breweries greater contractual freedom than they have under the current specific exemption for this sector. secondly, the proposed block exemption does not presuppose that non-compete agreements with a brewery with a market share of more than 30% are illegal. a brewery which achieves such a market share may notify its non-competition agreements to the commission. the commission will therefore first assess the actual impact of the agreements on competition. if the impact is significant, the commission may in any event take into account the economic benefits arising from such non-competition agreements when assessing the possible applicability to such agreements of an individual exemption under article 81 (3). thirdly, if an individual derogation is not applied to these agreements, the commission will examine possible solutions to be applied within the current distribution system. in other words, the commission will in principle try to solve any competition problems by first amending existing agreements and taking account of the economic benefits arising from them. the honourable member will certainly agree that the commission, as the european competition authority, must assess with particular care agreements concluded by operators with a significant market share. since these agreements may lead to market closure, they are in fact capable of harming competition not only at the level of producers in other member states but also at the level of small belgian breweries. this is also why the commission recently launched an investigation into interbrew. in conclusion, mr president, the commission does not believe that the new policy on vertical restraints can bring about major structural changes in the beer sector and in the hotel and catering sector in belgium, changes which could endanger the beer culture in that country.
commission - (it) mr beysen, i agree with you, information is important in this area too. the commission has therefore followed the policy of openness in the field of information in formulating the proposal for a regulation in question. we are in the process of examining the replies which have been submitted to us by all the interested parties following the publication of this proposal in the official journal. once this assessment has been made, we will consult the member states again. we intend to adopt the new regulation before the end of the year. we have communicated all the passages as fully as possible and therefore we feel that we have fulfilled our duty of information and consultation. of course, the commission is always ready to clarify any aspect which may still be unclear.

the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. i appreciate the importance of this and i was determined to be present. i had a seat on the flight this morning, but due to bad weather conditions in brussels, the flight has unfortunately been cancelled. in fact, my next flight was delayed as well. i should like to apologize for the delay and for the fact that other members pointed out that the commission took a long time to initiate the infringement procedure against france, which it finally did on 16 november. the letter of formal notice, the most factual part of the procedure, and yesterday, the adoption by parliament of the reasoned opinion which must be sent to france and which provides for a five-day time limit for replying. let me say this. i am firmly convinced that the line i took in trying to solve this problem was the right one. i have no doubt about that. there are many reasons for this, which i have already mentioned here in the committees of this parliament. a settlement negotiated between the parties is always preferable to an infringement procedure. however, it was alleged that the commission had, by adopting this approach, delayed the initiation of the infringement procedure, which would have delayed the hearing. it's not fair. it's not fair. the truth is that france did not take a clear position on this matter until 1 october. at that time, i had been in the position for only two weeks. this was the first occasion for the commission, or rather for me, to examine seriously the french reaction to this case. i tried to resolve this conflict in any way that seemed appropriate. so, as the person responsible for consumer protection, public health and food safety, my first reaction was to see if this claim was founded. have the french authorities been in possession of any evidence which the scientific steering committee of the commission should examine? you will remember that i asked the french authorities to send this evidence to the scientific steering committee so that it could also be evaluated and see if anything new could be discovered. the french authorities have done so and the scientific steering committee has also asked the british authorities to send it the updated information they have. they, too, have been executed. this has allowed the scientific steering committee to review all the evidence related to this unfortunate case in depth. we all know what his conclusions were. as regards my own responsibilities, which i have just mentioned, i thought that this was an important first step in this case. the opinion i received, which i was happy to follow, stated that beef exported from the united kingdom under the date-based export scheme was as safe as any other beef from the european union. other discussions followed. in my view, these discussions and the memorandum of understanding concluded between the parties and the experts concerned have given more assurance to consumers in the european union - and they are not only french - that beef exported under the date-based export regime is as safe as any beef from the european union. that is also very positive. as to whether there has been a delay or whether the infringement procedure will reach the court later than it would have been if the letter of formal notice had been chosen, the first letter sent by the commission normally requires a time limit of two months for reply. in the present case, this period was reduced to two weeks, after an additional week was granted following a request from the french authorities. the reasoned opinion, when sent two months after the letter of formal notice, normally also grants a two-month period for reply. the procedure adopted by the commission has reduced these delays. so we caught up and we are no further behind than if we had followed the normal procedures. i therefore believe not only that we have taken a good approach, which has produced positive results, but i also firmly believe that no delay can be attributed to us for having taken this approach. mr stevenson also spoke of germany's position. i believe that this will be discussed in the german parliament on 17 december. we really hope that the conclusions of parliament will be in favour of lifting the embargo in germany as well. i now turn to some of the points raised by mrs roth-behrendt and mr graefe zu baringdorf, which concern mainly the tests to be carried out. you will recall that these points were raised by the french authorities and dealt with in the memorandum of understanding. last september, at my hearing, i said that i intended to establish a reliable bse test in europe to determine the levels of infectiousness in the various member states. i still intend to. progress has been made. a working group has been set up in my directorate-general, a group which works in association with the member states and which is responsible for presenting the procedures necessary to put this provision into effect. i mean, keep going in that direction. mr graefe zu baringdorf and others also mentioned the need to set up labelling systems and, in particular, mandatory labelling systems. we'll discuss this later in the evening. let me just say at this point that labelling is a consumer information and choice issue, not a public health issue. we need to focus on the health aspect of this issue. that is why i believe that food safety testing is important and should be distinguished from the need for labelling. other members asked questions about the court's procedures, how quickly they are engaged and when a result can be expected. like all court proceedings in the world, it proceeds at its own pace because it is absolutely essential that all parties present their arguments in writing. in the event of a dispute being brought before the european court of justice, not only are the proceedings directly between the two parties - the commission and france in this case - but the member states are also perfectly entitled to intervene in the proceedings in question: the united kingdom or even any other member state. therefore, additional documents should be drawn up, in which member states would describe their position. all must be forwarded to the court and translated. all of this takes time. some have asked whether procedures could not be applied urgently in this case. there is an interim procedure but the criteria for applying interim measures are relatively strict and narrow. i asked the commission's legal service whether these particular circumstances meet these narrow criteria. i think that the battle will be difficult to some extent, but i would nevertheless like to ask the opinion of this service. if i am told that this is the right way to proceed, i intend to go that way. if the embargo is maintained and if the infringement procedure is launched next week, then, of course, this procedure will have to be launched before a decision on interim measures is taken. the legal service and i will also have to define the appropriate response to the french authorities' response to the reasoned opinion we have agreed, since it is essentially a legal document setting out the legal position. i hope that the answer we receive will be of the same nature. we cannot make any final decisions on interim measures until these documents have been filed. there is another procedure, which is very rare: the accelerated procedure. i asked if this procedure could be used. this procedure would allow the commission to ask the court to deal with the case in an expedited manner - or as a matter of urgency. in order to be able to follow this procedure, certain criteria must once again be met. it also requires the commission to give up, for example, its right to file certain documents at certain crucial stages of the case. i have to decide whether it is worthwhile to try to meet those criteria if we can, and if so, whether it is good to want an early oral procedure or whether it is better to have all the arguments in writing before the court. that is a judgment which i will have to make after reading the reply to the reasoned opinion which was sent to the french authorities. however, if i come to the conclusion that this is the way to go, that is the course i intend to take. i would just like to return to the issue of mandatory labelling and traceability, which was mentioned earlier by a member of the house. the date-based export regime is in itself a guarantee of traceability. it therefore also provides guarantees for labelling. this requirement was part of that regime. it would therefore be wrong to approach this debate by claiming that the date-based export regime did not require the establishment of these elements. that would be unfair to the scientists who have defined what is necessary to ensure that uk beef exports are completely safe and it would be unfair to the commission given the approach it has taken so far. this scheme provides guarantees as regards traceability and, consequently, labelling. a number of speakers also asked me about the progress of the food safety agency and the development of the white paper on food safety. in the opinion of several members, and i share that opinion, this seems to be the way forward in dealing with these matters. i think many of you will agree that it's really not good to be in a situation where scientists disagree on issues as important as food security. this is not satisfactory from the point of view of public health but also from the point of view of consumer confidence. this is not a desirable situation. from the very beginning of this commission, president prodi, as you will remember, has always said that this is a matter of crucial importance. even before we all took the oath, he put this issue at the top of his priorities. he asked me to take care of it. my general management has been working on this matter ever since. the white paper has been drawn up, it has been the subject of cross-departmental consultation within the commission and it is about to be presented to my colleagues in the college of commissioners. i hope that will be done on january 12. the white paper contains many of the subjects which i have often discussed here and in the committee on the environment. but it also includes a chapter on the establishment of a competent authority for food safety. i think that if we are to establish a food safety authority, we will need to define its powers. it will certainly be responsible for the risk assessment and when the scientists of this agency assess these risks, they will not only have to follow their own advice but they will also have to consult the scientists of the member states. such an agency - authority or agency, whatever - will not only have to be independent but will also have to work in liaison with the scientists of the member states. we must avoid the work of this agency becoming a series of orders from brussels as to the best way forward. such an agency will only gain the confidence of member states and consumers if it ensures a high degree of consultation between scientists in the european union. but once the consultation process is complete, once the scientists of the member states and the agency have reached a conclusion indicating the best course of action in a given situation, especially with regard to food concerns, the opinion of the agency cannot be changed, it must be respected, followed and cannot be questioned. once the consultation process is completed, there should be no need to question it. this is how the authority of such an agency will be established throughout the european union and how it will not only be effective in the field of public safety and health but also how it will gain the trust of consumers, which i believe is absolutely necessary. it will thus be the basis for all progress. i would like to refer very briefly to the other point we discussed a moment ago: the courts and tribunals. the hierarchy of procedures at the level of courts and tribunals is such that you could not for a moment imagine that an appeal court in any member state would seek the opinion of the court of justice of luxembourg by reference to article 177 and then, once in possession of the opinion, deem it inappropriate and say: 'we will not apply it'. that's not possible. there is no such thing in the scientific world.

- question no 9 by mr miguel angel martínez martínez (h-0697/99) subject: 50th anniversary of the geneva conventions in the context of the 50th anniversary of the geneva conventions and in view of the armed conflicts that have erupted in the world in recent years, particularly those on the european continent, what comments can the council make on the degree of respect for international humanitarian law as referred to in the abovementioned geneva conventions?
counsel. - (fi) mr president, even as the fiftieth anniversary of the four geneva conventions was being celebrated in august 1999, the european union confirmed its commitment to promoting international humanitarian law in all armed conflicts. the finnish presidency stressed that the european union was committed to respecting the four conventions and the two geneva protocols, which were the basic agreements in this field. the european union has invited those countries which have not yet ratified the geneva conventions and other agreements in the humanitarian field to do so in the near future. where necessary, the european union has also stressed, in a bilateral context, to countries involved in conflicts the need for full compliance with the provisions of these conventions. at the 27th international conference of the red cross and red crescent, held from 30 october to 16 november 1999, the european union issued a joint statement for the first time in which it stressed that recent and ongoing conflicts had demonstrated that war increasingly targets civilians, in particular women and children, or uses them as a direct extension of the conflict. the european union expressed its concern at the seriousness of the situation and expressed its deep regret at the continued violations of international humanitarian law. in this regard, the european union welcomed the report published by the un secretary-general on the protection of civilians in armed conflict. many of the secretary-general's important recommendations need to be addressed rapidly and provide a good basis for the security council to take an active role in this regard. in order to ensure more effective implementation of international humanitarian law, the european union has provided a common guarantee on handguns, small arms and anti-personnel mines. in addition, at its meeting on 11 november 1999, the council expressed its serious concern at the continuation of hostilities in the north caucasus. in this regard, the european union has already condemned the disproportionate and arbitrary use of violence in chechnya, which has caused enormous suffering among the civilian population. the council urges all the belligerents to respect international humanitarian law. the council also called on the russian government in particular to avoid causing civilian casualties and to ensure that any obstacles to international humanitarian aid were removed, including for the growing number of people who had to flee their region of residence to ingushetia. the geneva conventions themselves have a preventive effect and those who may be guilty of violations of humanitarian law are increasingly aware that their impunity is no longer a given. the european union has repeatedly stated that impunity cannot be accepted. if national methods are not effective enough, it is the international community that is ultimately responsible for enforcing the law. legal cases relating to violations of international humanitarian law are therefore an important tool to promote compliance with the conventions. the international tribunals for the former yugoslavia and rwanda have underlined the importance of the geneva conventions in increasing the credibility of the concepts of war crimes and individual responsibility. in this regard, the european union welcomes the approval of the statute of the international criminal court. it has always been committed to the early entry into force of the rome statute and the establishment of an effective and credible international criminal court. the european union is of the opinion that in the future the main objective of the international community must be to bridge the growing gap between existing international standards and their respect. the european union is determined to ensure that this specific approach to humanitarian issues is included in the agenda of international forums. at the 54th session of the united nations general assembly, the presidency called on the international community to find appropriate solutions and responses to new and unforeseen challenges in humanitarian law.

counsel. - (fi) mr president, in accordance with articles 321 of the ec treaty, 33 of the euratom treaty and 29 of the ecsc treaty, the decisionmaking process of the court of justice of the european communities is and will remain secret. in practice, only the court of justice of the european communities applies these provisions. in accordance with articles 245 of the ec treaty, 45 of the ecsc treaty and 160 of the euratom treaty, the council may amend these provisions only at the request of the court of justice of the european communities. the idea put forward by the honourable member is of course one of the approaches that can be applied when we evaluate, in practice, how to implement the opening up of the decisionmaking process of a legal body. however, as the honourable member very rightly points out, this is not a practice that is applied by the systems of all the member states. the approach proposed by the honourable member has advantages and disadvantages, as does the approach used under the current legislation applicable to the court of justice of the european communities. we may feel, however, that in view of the delicate stability to be sought in this area, the various principles to be followed in this case must be adequately respected.

commission. - mr president, i should like to begin by thanking you. some members are very familiar with the matter. the commission's proposal for a directive on late payment contains a package of measures to combat late payment in commercial transactions within the european union. the directive applies to late payment between all companies, including those in the public sector. it provides the legal framework to discourage late payment or the imposition of excessively long payment periods on businesses. it also makes debt recovery procedures faster and more efficient. the common position adopted by the council in july this year reduces the six operational articles of our proposal to two. i am aware that the member states have difficulty accepting changes to their legislation. the commission has nevertheless indicated that it would like a more ambitious approach to late payment. if the directive does not contain ambitious provisions, it will not achieve its objective. i therefore welcome the interest shown by parliament in our proposal and congratulate the rapporteur, mr murphy, and the coordinators of the other political groups on their excellent work. as regards the proposed amendments, i welcome most of them because they revive many of the commission's original proposals and try to fill in the gaps in the common position. in this respect, the commission can 20 and 25. we would like in particular to reduce the number of reports which the commission should produce under amendment no 25. it is better to use this time to pay bills more quickly, as mr maccormick has pointed out. finally, the commission cannot accept certain amendments for specific reasons. these are amendments nos 2, 18 and 23. mrs thyssen has just spoken about amendment no 18. we do not think that the council will accept this amendment concerning the obligation for the buyer to provide a bill of exchange in the event of a long contractual period of payment. in fact, it seems that this amendment is based on the law of a member state and that the proposed rule has not worked very well in that state so far. the 15 member states therefore opposed the proposal. we would also prefer not to amend article 4 on the duration of recovery procedures. the council's discussions were very tough in this respect. we think the result is satisfactory. by reducing the period from 90 to 60 days, as proposed in amendment no 23, we risk having the council return to the old version of the commission proposal and exclude the period which the debtor needs to defend himself. that would add about 30 days in most countries and the result would be similar to what we have now. in short, the commission expects this proposal to be very positive for businesses, especially smes. reducing late payment will improve the cash flow of companies. it will also reduce the financial burden of late payment and the high administrative cost of debt collection. i hope that early next year we can return to more general questions of company policy. europe needs a new business policy climate and an environment where it is easier, cheaper and more encouraging to set up small and medium-sized enterprises. only in this way will europe be able to reduce the unemployment figures which are too high. we need a strong and growing sme sector. let this proposal contribute to this new approach. the council has already banned the placing on the market and use of bst for dairy cows in 1990 in accordance with council decision 90/218/eec. in 1994, the council extended the moratorium until 31 december 1999. this is council decision 94/936/ec. article 2 of decision 94/936/ec provided that the commission was to entrust a group of independent scientists with the task of assessing the effects of the use of bst. before putting a new proposal on the council's table, the commission awaited the opinions of the two scientific committees, which were issued on 18 march 1999. the scientific committee on veterinary measures in relation to public health recognised potential links with prostate and breast cancers and, in the absence of evidence, indicated that further studies were needed. secondary risks are possible: allergic reactions and increased use of antimicrobial substances. the lack of evidence will require the commission to monitor very closely all scientific research on the risks to human health which the ingestion of products from bst-treated dairy cows may pose and, if necessary, to recommend additional preventive measures. having adopted its report on the impact of the use of bovine somatotropin on animal welfare on 10 march 1999, the scientific committee on animal health and welfare stated that bst increases the risk of clinical mastitis and the duration of its treatment, that it also increases the risk of foot and limb diseases and that it may adversely affect reproduction and cause severe injection site reactions. the cssba therefore considered that bst should not be administered to dairy cows. the protocol on protection and welfare of animals annexed to the treaty establishing the european community calls on the community and the member states to take full account of animal health and welfare requirements when formulating and implementing the common agricultural policy. by decision 78/923/eec the community approved the european convention for the protection of animals kept for farming purposes. all member states have also ratified this convention. council directive 98/58/ec on the protection of animals kept for farming purposes states that no substance, other than substances administered for therapeutic or prophylactic purposes, should be administered to an animal unless it has been demonstrated, by scientific animal welfare studies or on the basis of experience, that the effect of the substance does not adversely affect its health or welfare. bst is not used in farms for therapeutic purposes, but only to improve milk production, and is harmful to animals. in the light of the opinion of the scientific committee on animal health and welfare, the commission - on my advice, at its meeting on 28 october - adopted a decision proposing a permanent ban on the marketing and use of bst in the community as from 1 january 2000, in accordance with the provisions of council directive 98/58/ec on the protection of animals kept for farming purposes. for the sake of clarity, i will say that bst is not marketed in europe but is produced here. there is only one company producing bst in the european union. only its export to third countries is permitted. its marketing is prohibited within the eu. i would add that any attempt to prohibit its production for export to third countries would have no legal basis and would not be within the commission's competence.

commission (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, once again on behalf of the commission i should like to welcome the fact that the european parliament is dealing with this subject this afternoon. i think it is very important that we show that the dramatic violations of human rights, as we have experienced and still experience in sierra leone, concern us as europeans, because human rights and human dignity throughout the world are indivisible for us and because we do not want to tolerate this selective perception that we are more affected by acts of violence close to us than by explosions of violence such as we have experienced for many years in sierra leone. i agree with those who have said that there are few conflicts in the world as barbaric, as bloody and unfortunately as hopeless - as far as a political solution is concerned - as this conflict in sierra leone. the european union welcomed the signing of the peace agreement in july. we have called on the parties to participate in its implementation and we have declared ourselves ready to do so. we knew it would be very difficult. we were aware that all the conditions for a functioning, stable and democratic rule of law in sierra leone had to be created in the first place and that the willingness to cooperate was limited. like parliament, we are therefore extremely concerned about the latest violations of the ceasefire and we are concerned that the peace agreement is only being applied very slowly - when it is being applied. but we must ask ourselves what we can do to help the victims of this conflict. the mere fact that the situation is so terrible does not help us much. that is why we are finally providing concrete assistance for reintegration with the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration programme. since 1997, the commission has been financing the restoration of social and economic infrastructure destroyed by the war through its rehabilitation programme. this programme provides jobs and income for families moving in and for veterans. a larger programme, worth some €20 million, is currently being worked on to support reconstruction and reintegration. it is intended to replace the current programme, which will expire in the middle of next year. other support for the re-establishment of agricultural communities is provided in the form of agricultural production aids and financed from the food security budget line. echo will continue to provide humanitarian aid. in 1999, ngos and un organisations received €14 million for the war-affected population. this includes aid to sierra leone - to refugees in neighbouring countries, liberia and guinea - and, as has been said here, aid to ngos that provide psychosocial support in refugee camps, have launched programmes to help demobilised child soldiers and are addressing this particularly horrible problem of child mutilation, in order to offer them a perspective on life. the member has just said that these children have no prospects. i don't think we should settle for it, but we should do everything we can to give these children a life worthy of a human being, no matter what. i would like to remind you that the extent of humanitarian aid in sierra leone does not depend on the means available, but on the state of security in the country. at the moment, aid organisations are severely limited in their work by the insecurity in the northern and western provinces of the country. the arrival of unamsl forces - the un mission in sierra leone - will be crucial in giving a new impetus to the disarmament process and thus improving security. other commission aid for the year 2000 is currently being prepared. we are in discussions with unicef and the ministry of social affairs, but also with various civil society groups, for additional support for children who are victims of war. i would like to emphasize here explicitly that the commission will always be ready to examine the proposals of these groups for action in the field of human rights. the commission is also prepared to study the possibility of financing the future truth and reconciliation commission from its budget line for human rights and democracy.

- the next item is the report (a5-0089/1999) by mrs redondo jiménez, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a european parliament and council decision amending decision 96/411/ec on the improvement of community agricultural statistics (com (99) 332 - c5-0042/1999 - 1999/0137 (cod)).
the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, the commission proposes to extend decision 96/411 until 2002, to delete certain articles in order to simplify its application and to avoid the member states being unable to receive an advance of 30% of the community contribution, all this under a codecision procedure. in 1997, the same decision was amended to extend by two years the time limit for member states to submit their reports and the time limit for the commission to prepare the progress report on the implementation of the procedure for the parliament and the council. given the importance of the common agricultural policy, reliable data for all is essential when important decisions have to be taken. therefore, each institution must give priority to the means of making these data ever more complete, reliable and rapid, so that agricultural statistics must be ever more flexible, harmonized and show more cohesion with other statistical areas while offering the possibility of integrating new sources. this requires firstly identifying areas where rationalisation measures can be taken, secondly identifying areas where there are new or growing needs and thirdly identifying the general criteria which will create the framework for the actions to be taken. at this stage of the procedure, it should no longer be necessary to indicate that all member states are expected to participate in these actions. but it 's not like that . the project is submitted on a voluntary basis to the member states. i would like to stress that this parliament has some difficulty in accepting that a member state can say 'i am not interested, i am not involved'. the common agricultural policy concerns all the member states, it affects us all. i would therefore like the commission and the council to review their copy so that the next proposal to this parliament establishes the mandatory application of this decision in all member states, with a single legal basis in the statistical field. i would like to discuss another aspect with the commission and the council; it concerns amendment no 5, which i hope will be taken into account given the data it requires, in accordance with regulation (ec) no 1390/99, which entered into force on 23 november 1999 and which states in article 2 that 'each member state shall make available to the commission all the data per budget item concerned which it receives at the request of the commission within a maximum period of 30 days'. i therefore ask the commission to make an explicit commitment to define each year, in the framework of the priority technical action plans proposed to it by the standing committee on agricultural statistics, the points identified in amendments nos 4 and 5, otherwise the co-decision process would be lengthened, which would make it difficult for the member states to draw up statistical reports. i therefore await the commission's reply on this point.
the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens. it provides for adoption on the basis of the codecision procedure. the proposal for your approval today is the first example of agricultural statistics to date. i thank the rapporteur, mrs redondo jiménez, for her excellent work and in particular for her cooperation with the council and the commission on this matter. the commission welcomes the general support expressed in the report for the draft council and parliament decision. it is based on council decision 96/411 (ec) on the improvement of community agricultural statistics. it provides the commission with a flexible tool to adapt statistical applications to the information it needs. this has helped to adapt the community agricultural statistics system to developments in the common agricultural policy. in its report to the european parliament and the council, the commission presented an overview of the actions undertaken in various fields during the period 1996-1999. the overall assessment of these actions by the commission is positive. however, the process of adapting national statistical systems to the needs arising from the reform of the common agricultural policy is not yet complete. the commission has therefore proposed, with some minor amendments, to extend the validity of decision 96/411 (ec) for a further three years. the main changes are either to simplify the implementation of this action programme or to reduce the time taken to pay community contributions. it is important to ensure that this new decision enters into force as soon as possible in order to avoid any gaps in the current legislation. efforts should be made to ensure that this proposal is adopted at first reading. as regards the report by mrs redondo jiménez, the commission can accept amendments nos 1, 2 and 3. on the other hand, the commission cannot accept amendment no 4, even in its new amended version. this amendment would imply new obligations for the member states which have not yet been discussed in the council, which would certainly prevent the council from adopting the proposal at first reading. the commission nevertheless agrees with the rapporteur that the additional information requested by this amendment would indeed be useful in order to get a better idea of the distribution of aid paid under the common agricultural policy. in order to encourage progress in this area, the commission is therefore committed to including such actions in the next technical programmes to start in 2001. we hope that this will reassure the european parliament of our intentions and encourage mrs redondo jiménez to withdraw this amendment in order to allow the proposal to be adopted at first reading.
the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, i should like to point out to the commission that this is not an amendment by the rapporteur but an amendment by the committee on agriculture, and that it is therefore voted on in committee and that, according to the rules of procedure, it cannot be withdrawn. amendment no 5, which would make amendment no 4 unnecessary - an amendment which i hope the commission will accept - concerns the commission only and not the council. its content is already governed by regulation 2390/99, which is about to enter into force. the amendment does not impose any other obligations on the commission. i therefore hope that the commission will accept it, because we have done everything possible to ensure that this proposal is adopted at first reading.
commission - mr president, a brief comment on amendment no 5. unfortunately, we are not in a position to accept amendment no 5 because we know that the council would not accept it.

- the next item is the report (a5-0093/1999) by mr savary, on behalf of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, on the proposal for a council decision amending decision 97/787/ec granting exceptional financial assistance to armenia and georgia with a view to extending it to tajikistan (com (99) 391 - c5-00171/1999 - 1999/0172 (cns)).
commission. - (sv) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by expressing my warm thanks to the rapporteur, mr savary. the commission notes with satisfaction that its proposal to grant exceptional financial support to tajikistan has been fully endorsed by the relevant parliamentary committee. it supports most of the proposed amendments, in particular those providing for stricter budgetary control in the event of a negative political development in the country, and also accepts the idea of a final report to be submitted to parliament in 2004. the commission cannot accept the amendments which concern the part of the aid to be granted in the form of a grant. it is not possible to base this donation on the existing legal basis, in particular in the context of the tacis programme, since the financial means allocated to support tajikistan cannot be allocated to different projects or programmes. the aim is to reduce the country's debt to the eu. the proposal also confirms the eur 95 million aid for armenia and georgia which was released following decision 97/787/ec of 17 november 1997. the commission finds it difficult to accept that the donation can be reduced to eur 50 million. the reason for this is that the union's financial commitment will remain high in this region whose stability is under threat, both because of the russian financial crisis and the current situation in the north caucasus. a significant reduction has already taken place, bringing the eu aid from an initial €212 million, including interest on outstanding debt, to the current amount of €123 million. however, a further reduction may occur in the next few years if the aid is implemented as planned. armenia and georgia will find it difficult to understand that the union is reducing its aid despite the significant efforts made by these two countries, with the help of the imf, among others, to reduce their debts to the union. this would put the eu in a difficult position vis-à-vis these countries and the international community. the commission considers it would be regrettable if the eu refused to confirm its financial assistance to countries whose strategic importance to our union is clear. in addition, the current difficulties in the caucasus region should encourage us to send political messages to the countries concerned that we remain ready to support their important efforts to achieve stability, democracy and reform.
